meta.title: Micro & Macroeconomics
meta.description: 350 MCQs covering micro and macroeconomics fundamentals for banking, built for the Entry Level Training Program.

questionBank.q: Economics is best defined as the study of how individuals and societies do what with limited resources?
opts: Distribute unlimited resources to satisfy limited wants
Allocate limited resources to satisfy unlimited wants
Regulate government spending on public projects
Forecast future prices of goods and services
questionBank.exp: Economics is defined as the study of how individuals and societies allocate limited resources to satisfy unlimited wants.

questionBank.q: A young professional weighs buying a new phone today against investing the same amount for future growth. Which concept guides her comparison?
opts: Market equilibrium
Opportunity cost
Elasticity of demand
Fiscal deficit
questionBank.exp: The manual uses this exact type of trade-off (luxury item now vs. saving/investing) to introduce opportunity cost.

questionBank.q: Why do employers in competitive job markets often value candidates with a background in economics?
opts: It shortens the standard interview process at most banks
It signals strong data analysis and market-trend skills
It substitutes for technical banking certifications during recruitment
It confirms proficiency in a specific foreign language
questionBank.exp: Employers seek candidates who can analyze data, understand market trends, and make strategic decisions — skills rooted in economics.

questionBank.q: A shopper delays buying rice because prices typically fall after the harvest season. Which everyday application of economics is this?
opts: Using opportunity cost to select a store loyalty program
Using supply and demand patterns to time a purchase
Using currency exchange trends to plan foreign travel
Using fiscal policy forecasts to negotiate a salary
questionBank.exp: Understanding supply and demand helps consumers identify low-demand periods for cost savings on purchases.

questionBank.q: A prospective homeowner researches how borrowing costs change over time before applying for a loan. This best illustrates economics applied to which personal goal?
opts: Planning for retirement using fiscal deficit projections
Planning for a major purchase using interest-rate awareness
Planning a vacation budget using exchange-rate history
Planning a career change using labor-supply statistics
questionBank.exp: Understanding mortgage/interest rates and their effect on monthly payments is crucial for major purchase decisions like homeownership.

questionBank.q: An employee travelling abroad checks how much local currency her salary converts to before the trip. Which economic benefit does this represent?
opts: Civic engagement through understanding tax policy
Global awareness through understanding currency movements
Risk assessment through understanding loan default rates
Product design through understanding customer segments
questionBank.exp: Understanding exchange rates and currency markets helps during international travel — an example of the global-awareness benefit.

questionBank.q: A citizen reads about a proposed change in government spending before voting in an election. Which benefit of economic literacy is being demonstrated?
opts: Financial decision-making through informed evaluation of loan offers
Civic engagement through informed evaluation of policy proposals
Career development through informed evaluation of job openings
Consumer choice through informed evaluation of product prices
questionBank.exp: Economics influences public policy; economic literacy lets citizens assess policy proposals and make informed voting choices.

questionBank.q: Which core banking function relies most directly on economic principles to decide who receives funding?
opts: Physical branch security oversight
Lending and investment allocation
Routine payroll administration processing
General office facilities management
questionBank.exp: Economic principles directly guide the allocation of funds to borrowers and investment opportunities.

questionBank.q: A bank studies how rising school fees affect household budgets before launching a new savings account. This reflects which banking application of economics?
opts: Designing marketing slogans based on brand color psychology
Designing customer-centric products based on economic behavior
Designing office layouts based on employee commute times
Designing IT systems based on server storage capacity
questionBank.exp: Understanding customer behavior, shaped by economics, is essential for designing products that meet real financial needs.

questionBank.q: Why is an understanding of economic trends critical when a bank assesses the risk of a business loan?
opts: It reduces documentation requirements for first-time borrowers
It helps predict a borrower's repayment ability as conditions change
It shortens the standard loan-approval timeline by default
It confirms the exact interest rate a competitor bank charges
questionBank.exp: Economic insights are crucial for assessing and mitigating risks related to lending decisions.

questionBank.q: How do economic trends such as inflation typically affect a bank's profitability?
opts: They directly influence capital adequacy ratios set by regulators
They directly influence lending rates and net interest income
They directly influence the bank's core banking software licensing fees
They directly influence the number of ATMs a bank can install
questionBank.exp: Economic trends directly impact interest rates, inflation, and exchange rates, which in turn affect a bank's profitability.

questionBank.q: In a Sub-Saharan African country experiencing high inflation, a bank raises its lending rates. What is the most likely effect on customer borrowing behavior?
opts: Customers immediately switch to a different national currency
Customers seek fewer loans or alternative financing options
Customers demand the central bank lower reserve requirements
Customers relocate their accounts to foreign-owned banks
questionBank.exp: Per the manual's SSA example, high lending rates make borrowing more expensive, so customers opt for fewer loans or alternative financing.

questionBank.q: When the Naira depreciates sharply against the US dollar, which change in customer behavior is most likely at a bank with import-dependent clients?
opts: Increased demand for extended weekend branch operating hours
Increased demand for foreign currency accounts to hedge exposure
Increased demand for physical cheque book issuance services
Increased demand for paper-based loan application processing systems
questionBank.exp: Customers exposed to currency depreciation seek foreign currency accounts to hedge, per the manual's currency-depreciation example.

questionBank.q: During a period of economic uncertainty, how do bank customers typically adjust their financial behavior?
opts: They increase spending and reduce savings
They increase savings and reduce borrowing
They increase borrowing and reduce loan repayments
They increase investment risk and reduce cash holdings
questionBank.exp: During downturns, customers become more cautious — increasing savings and reducing borrowing — affecting deposit and lending activity.

questionBank.q: A government introduces stricter know-your-customer requirements for opening bank accounts. How does this typically affect customer interaction with banks?
opts: Customers receive automatic interest-rate discounts on new accounts
Customers face more rigorous documentation during account opening
Customers submit fewer identification documents than before
Customers gain priority access to newly launched foreign currency accounts
questionBank.exp: Stricter KYC regulations lead to more rigorous documentation processes for customers opening accounts.

questionBank.q: The rapid adoption of mobile money services like M-Pesa has most directly changed customer behavior in which way?
opts: Customers now prefer visiting physical branches for every transaction
Customers now prefer performing banking activities via mobile apps
Customers now prefer writing paper cheques for daily purchases
Customers now prefer holding cash reserves at home
questionBank.exp: Customers have embraced digital banking for convenience, reducing branch foot traffic in favor of mobile/online banking.

questionBank.q: In a customer-facing role, why does understanding a customer's economic circumstances matter most?
opts: It enables faster processing of unrelated internal paperwork
It enables tailored financial solutions suited to their situation
It enables stricter enforcement of unrelated dress code rules
It enables quicker scheduling of unrelated staff meetings
questionBank.exp: Understanding the economic realities customers face helps staff provide tailored financial solutions.

questionBank.q: Product development teams rely on economic insight primarily to achieve what outcome?
opts: Products that align with a competitor's office branding style
Products that align with customers' financial needs and preferences
Products that align with the bank's internal seating chart
Products that align with an unrelated software vendor's roadmap
questionBank.exp: Economic insights inform the creation of products that align with customers' financial needs and preferences.

questionBank.q: A bank analyst studies how a rise in national unemployment might affect overall loan demand across the country. Which branch of economics does this analysis belong to?
opts: Microeconomics, because it examines a single customer's account
Macroeconomics, because it examines the economy as a whole
Fiscal policy, because it examines government tax collection
Monetary policy, because it examines central bank reserve rules
questionBank.exp: Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole at the national and global level, unlike microeconomics' focus on individual behavior.

questionBank.q: A regulator drafts a policy specifically aimed at reducing national inflation and unemployment. Which category of economic policy does this fall under?
opts: Microeconomic policy aimed at single-firm price regulation
Macroeconomic policy aimed at whole-economy stabilization
Trade policy aimed at bilateral tariff negotiation
Consumer policy aimed at individual product labeling
questionBank.exp: Per the Micro vs. Macro comparison, macroeconomic policy targets economic growth, unemployment, and inflation control economy-wide.

questionBank.q: A newly recruited Access Bank officer asks why economics training is required even for staff outside the research and treasury units. Per the course's rationale, the most complete justification is that economics:
opts: Shapes decisions across customer service, risk management, product development and strategy, regardless of role
Helps only treasury and research staff price securities and forecast yields
Is a CBN-mandated training requirement rather than a tool for daily decision-making
Matters mainly to corporate bankers who negotiate pricing terms with large clients
questionBank.exp: The course frames economics as relevant across customer service, risk management, product development and strategic decision-making — not a specialist function reserved for a few departments.

questionBank.q: Access Bank's credit committee uses macroeconomic forecasts and sector outlooks, rather than only collateral values, before approving a large facility to a manufacturer. Per the course's discussion of economics' significance in banking, this practice is best described as:
opts: Customer-centric product design, since the loan is tailored to the manufacturer's needs
Interest rate and profit management, since the loan size affects net interest margin directly
Risk assessment, since the committee is solely evaluating the manufacturer's collateral value
Lending and investment decisions, since economic principles are guiding the allocation of bank funds
questionBank.exp: The course lists 'lending and investment decisions' as a distinct function where economic principles guide fund allocation. Option C is wrong because the stem describes macro/sector analysis, not a collateral-only review.

questionBank.q: Per the course's comparison table, which pairing correctly matches the LEVEL OF ANALYSIS for microeconomics and macroeconomics, respectively?
opts: Specific markets and industries; national and global economies
National and global economies; specific markets and industries
Individual transactions; regional government budgets only
Household behaviour; firm-level production decisions
questionBank.exp: The course's table places microeconomics at the level of specific markets and industries, and macroeconomics at the level of national and global economies.

questionBank.q: Which set of concepts is classified under MACROECONOMICS in the course's comparison table?
opts: Supply and demand, market equilibrium, elasticity, consumer surplus
GDP, inflation, unemployment, interest rates, economic growth, business cycles
Producer surplus, elasticity, market equilibrium, consumer surplus
Firm-level pricing, brand differentiation, market share, advertising spend
questionBank.exp: The table lists GDP, inflation, unemployment, interest rates, economic growth and business cycles under macroeconomics' key concepts.

questionBank.q: Per the course material, government policies aimed at promoting competition, regulating businesses and protecting consumers fall under the policy implications of:
opts: Macroeconomics, because all regulation ultimately affects national output
Fiscal policy exclusively, since regulation is funded through the national budget
Microeconomics, because these policies target specific markets, firms and consumer interactions
Monetary policy exclusively, since the CBN oversees all market regulation
questionBank.exp: The course's table assigns competition, business regulation and consumer protection policies to microeconomics' policy implications.

questionBank.q: An Access Bank regional head presents economic insights on Sub-Saharan African growth trends to the executive committee to support a market-expansion decision. This best reflects which banking role described in the course material?
opts: Strategy and decision-making, because economic insight is informing the bank's broader strategic planning
Customer service, because the regional head is responding to customer enquiries
Product development, because new account types are being launched
Risk management, because the focus is solely on individual loan defaults
questionBank.exp: The course lists 'strategy and decision-making' as the role where staff contribute economic insight to strategic planning.

questionBank.q: The course material describes economics as 'the bedrock of banking.' The strongest support for this claim, drawing on the course's own examples, is that:
opts: Bank profitability is determined solely by board-level marketing decisions, independent of economic conditions
Economic knowledge is useful mainly for understanding international news rather than daily operations
Economics is required only for staff who interact with the Central Bank of Nigeria directly
Lending, product design, risk assessment, and the pricing of loans and deposits are all directly shaped by economic trends
questionBank.exp: Across its examples, the course ties lending, product design, risk assessment and pricing decisions directly to economic indicators and trends.

questionBank.q: A Nigerian bank customer with a foreign-currency account suddenly increases their forex holdings significantly. According to the course, which economic event MOST LIKELY triggered this behaviour?
opts: A spike in domestic interest rates
Naira depreciation against the US dollar
The introduction of new KYC regulations
A regional economic boom in West Africa
questionBank.exp: The material directly states that when local currencies like the Naira devalue, customers with foreign-currency accounts or international trade exposure hedge by seeking more forex products — currency depreciation is the trigger.

questionBank.q: Economics is defined in this course as the study of how individuals and societies allocate their limited resources to satisfy unlimited wants. Under this definition, which scenario is STRICTLY a macroeconomic question?
opts: Why does the price of petrol at a specific station affect how many litres customers buy?
Should a company produce more smartphones or laptops given its factory capacity?
What is the effect of a 2% rise in Nigeria's MPR on national GDP growth?
How does a price subsidy change the quantity demanded of rice in Kano?
questionBank.exp: Macroeconomics focuses on the economy as a whole — national income, GDP, interest rates at the national level. The MPR's effect on GDP is a national/aggregate question. The others involve individual markets or firm-level decisions (microeconomics).

questionBank.q: A government implements stricter Know-Your-Customer (KYC) regulations. Which banking function does this MOST directly affect, and in what direction?
opts: Risk management — decreases credit risk by creating information barriers
Customer service — increases friction in account opening, altering customer interaction patterns
Product development — forces banks to create new loan products
Monetary policy transmission — reduces the CBN's ability to control money supply
questionBank.exp: The course example specifically notes that stricter KYC leads to more rigorous documentation processes, directly altering how customers interact with banks during account opening — a customer service friction issue, not a product or monetary issue.

questionBank.q: The course highlights M-Pesa in Kenya as a real-world example of how technological advances affect banking. What is the PRIMARY mechanism by which such innovations create competitive pressure on traditional banks?
opts: They lower the CBN's monetary policy rate
They shift customers away from physical branches toward digital platforms
They increase government KYC documentation requirements
They create new fiscal policy obligations for commercial banks
questionBank.exp: The course notes that M-Pesa and similar platforms led customers to prefer mobile/digital banking, reducing physical branch traffic and forcing banks to build better digital infrastructure — the pressure is channel substitution.

questionBank.q: A banker at Access Bank is advising a client considering a business loan during a period of high inflation in Nigeria. Which microeconomic and macroeconomic insight combination should guide the advice?
opts: High inflation → lower real returns; firm-level demand analysis irrelevant to risk
High inflation → CBN likely to raise MPR → higher borrowing costs; assess client's pricing power in their market
Currency depreciation → reduce lending; ignore the client's cost structure
Economic boom → lending is risk-free; no need for credit analysis
questionBank.exp: The correct approach combines macroeconomic insight (inflation triggers MPR hikes, raising borrowing costs) with microeconomic analysis (client's market position/pricing power determines ability to service debt despite higher costs).

questionBank.q: Scarcity in economics refers to which fundamental condition?
opts: Unlimited resources exceeding all possible wants
Limited resources unable to satisfy unlimited wants
Equal distribution of resources among all people
A temporary shortage caused by seasonal weather patterns
questionBank.exp: Scarcity is the basic economic problem of limited resource availability against unlimited human wants and needs.

questionBank.q: A sudden surge in population increases the need for housing beyond what is currently available. Which type of scarcity does this illustrate?
opts: Supply-induced scarcity
Demand-induced scarcity
Structural scarcity
Currency scarcity
questionBank.exp: Demand-induced scarcity occurs when demand for a good or service exceeds supply, e.g. due to population growth.

questionBank.q: The total amount of gold in the world limits how much can ever be mined. Which type of scarcity does this best illustrate?
opts: Demand-induced scarcity
Supply-induced scarcity
Structural scarcity
Opportunity-cost scarcity
questionBank.exp: Supply-induced scarcity results from natural or physical constraints, exactly as illustrated by the manual's gold example.

questionBank.q: Steel used in car manufacturing is mined in one region, while the rubber needed for tyres is grown in a distant region. Which type of scarcity does this illustrate?
opts: Demand-induced scarcity
Structural scarcity
Supply-induced scarcity
Seasonal scarcity
questionBank.exp: Structural scarcity occurs when resources needed for production aren't available in the same place — the manual's own steel/rubber example.

questionBank.q: Because resources cannot satisfy every want, individuals and societies are forced to do what?
opts: Reduce the total number of consumer choices available
Prioritize which needs and wants to satisfy first
Increase the total resource supply through taxation
Wait for supply-induced scarcity to resolve naturally
questionBank.exp: Scarcity creates the need for choice — since we can't have everything, we must prioritize our needs and wants.

questionBank.q: Scarcity often forces individuals or groups to compete for limited resources. Which form can this competition take, according to the material?
opts: Educational and technological competition
Economic, political, or military competition
Diplomatic and cultural competition
Recreational and sporting competition
questionBank.exp: Competition arising from scarcity can come in various forms, specifically economic, political, or military, per the material.

questionBank.q: How can scarcity contribute positively to an economy over time?
opts: It drives inflation as people seek more government subsidies
It drives innovation as people seek more efficient ways to produce
It drives unemployment as people seek fewer job opportunities
It drives migration as people seek unrelated tourism destinations
questionBank.exp: Scarcity can lead to innovation, as it pushes people to find more efficient production methods or new resource sources.

questionBank.q: Beyond competition, scarcity can also encourage which behavior among people facing a common resource shortage?
opts: Isolation to avoid sharing scarce resources
Cooperation to solve shared resource problems
Deregulation to increase resource production
Taxation to redistribute scarce resources
questionBank.exp: Scarcity can also engender cooperation, as people come together to solve common resource problems.

questionBank.q: Opportunity cost is best defined as which of the following?
opts: The total monetary cost of a chosen option
The value of the best alternative forgone
The government tax applied to a chosen option
The interest earned on a chosen investment
questionBank.exp: Opportunity cost is the value of what you give up when choosing one option over another.

questionBank.q: A student skips a part-time shift to study for an exam, losing no wages but losing study-free leisure time. Which type of opportunity cost is this?
opts: An explicit, monetary cost
An implicit, non-monetary cost
A structural scarcity cost
A demand-induced cost
questionBank.exp: Implicit costs are non-monetary, such as time — unlike explicit costs, which are easily measured in money.

questionBank.q: A company invests all available funds into building a new factory instead of funding a marketing campaign. What is the opportunity cost of this decision?
opts: The benefit that a new office renovation would have provided
The benefit that the marketing campaign would have provided
The benefit that a staff bonus scheme would have provided
The benefit that a corporate rebrand would have provided
questionBank.exp: The manual's own example: a company investing in a factory forgoes the benefit of alternatives such as marketing.

questionBank.q: A government allocates land to build a new expressway rather than a housing estate. What does this scenario best illustrate?
opts: The scarcity caused by a natural resource shortage
The opportunity cost of the government's land-use decision
The structural scarcity of construction materials
The demand-induced scarcity of housing land
questionBank.exp: The manual's own example: land used for an expressway forgoes the alternative use of housing estates — the opportunity cost.

questionBank.q: Why is it often difficult to apply opportunity cost to decisions like spending time with family rather than working?
opts: The forgone benefit does not actually exist in this case
The forgone benefit is hard to assign a monetary value to
The forgone benefit matches the explicit monetary cost exactly
The forgone benefit is irrelevant to economic decision-making
questionBank.exp: It can be difficult to put a monetary value on time with relatives or friends, even though the cost is still real and worth considering.

questionBank.q: A trade-off in economics arises directly from which underlying condition?
opts: The abundance of resources relative to limited wants
The scarcity of resources relative to unlimited wants
The equal distribution of income across society
The fixed exchange rate between two currencies
questionBank.exp: Trade-offs are an unavoidable part of decision-making because of the scarcity of resources and our inability to have everything we want.

questionBank.q: A curve showing the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce with available resources is known as what?
opts: Market equilibrium curve
Production possibilities frontier
Aggregate demand curve
Consumer indifference curve
questionBank.exp: The production possibilities frontier shows combinations of two goods producible with available resources and technology, highlighting trade-offs.

questionBank.q: An investor must decide between two projects without knowing which will succeed, and weighs the potential benefits and costs before choosing. Which concept does this illustrate?
opts: Structural scarcity
Choice under uncertainty
Explicit opportunity cost
Market equilibrium
questionBank.exp: Choice under uncertainty is deciding without knowing all possible outcomes, weighing potential benefits and costs before deciding.

questionBank.q: A consumer buys a new car, leaving less money available for rent and groceries. What economic principle is being demonstrated?
opts: A shortage caused by supply-induced scarcity
A trade-off between competing uses of limited income
A shift in the market equilibrium price
An increase in the consumer's opportunity cost of leisure
questionBank.exp: The manual's own example: buying a car means less money for other things like housing or food — a trade-off.

questionBank.q: A factory reallocates machinery to produce more refrigerators, resulting in fewer washing machines being produced. What does this best represent?
opts: A demand-induced scarcity in the appliance market
A trade-off along the production possibilities frontier
An implicit opportunity cost of factory rent
A structural scarcity in machinery availability
questionBank.exp: Producing more of one good at the expense of another is the trade-off the production possibilities frontier illustrates directly.

questionBank.q: A government raises its education budget, which requires reducing funds previously allocated to healthcare. What does this scenario best illustrate?
opts: A demand-induced scarcity of healthcare workers
A trade-off in government resource allocation
A supply-induced scarcity of school buildings
An implicit cost of the healthcare ministry's time
questionBank.exp: The manual's own example: spending more on education means spending less on healthcare or housing — a resource-allocation trade-off.

questionBank.q: Why are trade-offs described as an unavoidable feature of economic decision-making?
opts: Because governments regularly raise taxes on luxury imports
Because scarce resources make it impossible to have everything
Because markets tend to clear at a single equilibrium price
Because consumers generally prefer imported over local goods
questionBank.exp: Trade-offs are unavoidable because we cannot have everything we want given scarcity of resources.

questionBank.q: A surge in Nigeria's urban population sharply increases mortgage applications beyond what banks can fund from current deposits. Per the course's classification, this is an example of:
opts: Demand-induced scarcity, because population growth has pushed demand for mortgages above available supply
Supply-induced scarcity, because deposit funds are physically limited by nature
Structural scarcity, because mortgage funds exist elsewhere but cannot reach this market
Artificial scarcity, because the bank is deliberately restricting mortgage approvals
questionBank.exp: The course attributes population growth as a cause of demand-induced scarcity — demand exceeding supply.

questionBank.q: A Nigerian assembly plant has all the funding it needs to produce vehicles but cannot proceed because steel components are sourced from one region and rubber components from another, with limited transport links between them. This illustrates:
opts: Demand-induced scarcity, since vehicle demand exceeds what the plant can produce
Supply-induced scarcity, since steel and rubber are both naturally limited resources
Structural scarcity, since the required inputs are not available in the same location
Technological scarcity, since the plant lacks the equipment to combine the inputs
questionBank.exp: This mirrors the course's own steel-and-rubber car example of structural scarcity — resources exist but not in the same place.

questionBank.q: Limited physical bank-branch infrastructure in rural Nigeria pushed providers to develop mobile money platforms that bypass the need for brick-and-mortar branches. Per the course's discussion of scarcity's implications, this is primarily an example of:
opts: The need for competition, since multiple providers compete for the same customers
The need for cooperation, since providers had to jointly fund branch construction
The need for choice, since customers had to choose between competing mobile platforms
The need for innovation, since scarcity drove the development of a more efficient way to deliver services
questionBank.exp: The course lists innovation as a response to scarcity — finding new, more efficient ways to deliver goods or services.

questionBank.q: Three SMEs in the same local market all seek financing from the same limited pool of affordable bank credit, each emphasising their creditworthiness to secure approval. Per the course's discussion of scarcity's implications, this illustrates:
opts: The need for cooperation, since the SMEs are working together to access funds
The need for competition, since scarcity of affordable credit drives firms to compete for access to it
The need for innovation, since the SMEs are developing new credit products
The need for choice, since the bank must choose which SME to support based on profitability alone
questionBank.exp: The course lists competition as a direct implication of scarcity — firms competing for limited resources.

questionBank.q: The course material lists the Consumption Possibilities Frontier, alongside the Production Possibilities Frontier, as a type of trade-off in economic choices. This concept is most directly concerned with:
opts: The maximum combinations of goods and services a household can purchase given a limited budget
The maximum output a factory can physically produce given its machinery
The interest rate a bank charges on consumer loans
The government's total revenue from consumption taxes
questionBank.exp: The Consumption Possibilities Frontier is the consumer-side equivalent of the PPF, showing combinations of goods affordable within a budget constraint.

questionBank.q: Per the course material, 'choice under uncertainty' refers to a situation in which:
opts: A government sets prices directly to remove uncertainty from the market
A decision-maker must choose without knowing all outcomes, weighing benefits and costs on the best available estimate
A firm operates in a market with only one buyer and one seller
A consumer has unlimited information about all possible outcomes before deciding
questionBank.exp: The course defines choice under uncertainty as deciding without knowing all outcomes, weighing potential benefits and costs on the best estimate available.

questionBank.q: A company chooses to invest in a new factory rather than expanding its existing warehouse. The trade-off in this decision is the broader exchange of gaining factory capacity while losing warehouse expansion; the opportunity cost, more precisely, is:
opts: The total cost of constructing the new factory
The value of the warehouse expansion specifically, as the next-best alternative forgone
The combined value of every alternative the company considered, however unlikely
Identical to the trade-off and interchangeable with it in all contexts
questionBank.exp: Opportunity cost is precisely the value of the specific next-best alternative forgone, distinct from the broader trade-off.

questionBank.q: A treasury team weighing whether to deploy excess liquidity into Treasury Bills or into a new SME lending fund is fundamentally responding to which underlying economic reality described in the course material?
opts: Market equilibrium, since both options have identical expected returns
Structural scarcity specifically, since SME funds and T-Bill funds originate from different sources
The law of supply, since T-Bill yields are set by the CBN alone
Scarcity, since the available funds are limited and cannot be allocated to both options in full
questionBank.exp: Choosing between competing uses for a limited pool of funds is a direct expression of scarcity forcing a choice.

questionBank.q: Nigeria has the agricultural land and rainfall needed to produce far more rice than it currently does, but inadequate rural road networks prevent harvested rice from reaching processing mills before spoilage. Which option most precisely describes this situation, per the course's classification of scarcity?
opts: Demand-induced scarcity, since population growth has outpaced rice production
A simultaneous combination of demand-induced and supply-induced scarcity, with no structural element
Supply-induced scarcity, since rice itself is a naturally limited crop
Structural scarcity, since the resources exist but cannot reach where they are needed due to a logistical mismatch
questionBank.exp: Resources (land, rainfall, harvested crop) exist but cannot reach where needed due to a location/logistics mismatch — the course's definition of structural scarcity.

questionBank.q: A bank officer spends 3 hours processing loan documents instead of attending a professional development seminar. The seminar fee of N10,000 was already non-refundable. What is the OPPORTUNITY COST of choosing to process the loan documents?
opts: N10,000 — the sunk cost of the seminar fee
The time value of 3 hours of professional development foregone (implicit cost), NOT the sunk fee
The loan processing salary earned (explicit cost)
Zero, because the seminar money is already spent
questionBank.exp: The N10,000 is a sunk cost (already spent, irrelevant to the decision). The real opportunity cost is the implicit, non-monetary value of professional development foregone — the 3 hours of learning lost by processing loans instead.

questionBank.q: Gold is limited by the total amount that exists in the earth's crust. This best illustrates which type of scarcity?
opts: Demand-induced scarcity
Structural scarcity
Supply-induced scarcity
Regulatory scarcity
questionBank.exp: Supply-induced scarcity arises from natural or physical constraints on the quantity available. The course uses exactly this example — gold supply is limited by physical existence, not by demand exceeding supply or geographic mismatch.

questionBank.q: Which outcome of scarcity does NOT appear in the course material?
opts: The need for choice among competing wants
The need for innovation to find more efficient production
The need for cooperation to solve common problems
The need for complete market information before any decision
questionBank.exp: The course lists four implications of scarcity: the need for choice, competition, innovation, and cooperation. 'Complete market information before decisions' is a characteristic of perfect competition theory, NOT listed as an implication of scarcity.

questionBank.q: According to the Law of Demand, holding all else constant, how does quantity demanded respond to a fall in price?
opts: Quantity demanded decreases as price falls
Quantity demanded increases as price falls
Quantity demanded stays fixed regardless of price
Quantity demanded rises with falling production costs
questionBank.exp: The Law of Demand states an inverse relationship: quantity demanded increases as price decreases and vice versa.

questionBank.q: In the manual's illustration, the price of a dozen eggs drops from ₦25 to ₦10. What happens to the weekly quantity purchased?
opts: It falls from 400 crates to 200 crates
It rises from 200 crates to 400 crates
It rises from 300 crates to 500 crates
It stays constant at 300 crates
questionBank.exp: The manual's egg example shows weekly quantity purchased rising from 200 to 400 crates as price falls from ₦25 to ₦10.

questionBank.q: When a small change in price causes a large change in quantity demanded, economists describe demand as what?
opts: Inelastic
Elastic
Fixed
Regressive
questionBank.exp: Elasticity signifies a high level of responsiveness to price changes — this is what 'elastic' demand means.

questionBank.q: Despite frequent price increases, sales volumes of cigarettes and fuel change only slightly. What does this demonstrate?
opts: Elastic demand for these products
Inelastic demand for these products
A supply-induced scarcity of these products
A structural scarcity of these products
questionBank.exp: When price fluctuations cause only minor changes in quantity purchased, demand is described as inelastic — the manual's own fuel/cigarettes example.

questionBank.q: According to the Law of Supply, holding all else constant, how does quantity supplied respond to a rise in price?
opts: Quantity supplied decreases as price rises
Quantity supplied increases as price rises
Quantity supplied stays fixed regardless of price
Quantity supplied rises with falling production costs
questionBank.exp: The Law of Supply states a direct relationship: quantity supplied increases as price increases.

questionBank.q: In the manual's illustration, the price of a dozen eggs rises from ₦15 to ₦35. What happens to the weekly quantity sellers offer?
opts: It falls from 500 crates to 200 crates
It rises from 200 crates to 500 crates
It rises from 100 crates to 400 crates
It stays constant at 350 crates
questionBank.exp: The manual's supply example shows sellers' weekly offer rising from 200 to 500 crates as price rises from ₦15 to ₦35.

questionBank.q: The extent to which sellers increase quantity supplied in response to a price rise is referred to as what?
opts: Elasticity of demand
Elasticity of supply
Market equilibrium
Structural scarcity
questionBank.exp: How responsive sellers are to price changes is described as elasticity of supply.

questionBank.q: Supply is best described in economic terms as what?
opts: The propensity, or willingness, to buy at various prices
The propensity, or willingness, to sell at various prices
The legal requirement to sell at a fixed price
The total quantity produced regardless of price
questionBank.exp: Supply is the 'propensity to sell' — how willing and ready sellers are to offer a quantity for sale at various prices.

questionBank.q: Market equilibrium occurs at the point where which condition holds?
opts: Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
Quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
Quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
Price is set below production cost
questionBank.exp: Market equilibrium is the point where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied — no shortage or surplus exists.

questionBank.q: In the manual's egg market illustration, at what price do sellers offer exactly 300 crates a week, matching buyer demand?
opts: ₦15 per dozen
₦33 per dozen
₦25 per dozen
₦35 per dozen
questionBank.exp: The manual identifies ₦33 per dozen as the true equilibrium price, where 300 crates are supplied and demanded weekly.

questionBank.q: If the price of eggs is set below the equilibrium price, what results in the market?
opts: A surplus, since sellers want to sell more than buyers want
A shortage, since buyers want more than sellers offer
No change, since price does not affect quantity
A shift in the supply curve to the right
questionBank.exp: Any price lower than equilibrium results in buyers wanting to purchase more than is available — a shortage.

questionBank.q: If the price of eggs is set above the equilibrium price, what results in the market?
opts: A shortage, since buyers want more than sellers offer
A surplus, since sellers offer more than buyers want
No change, since price does not affect quantity
A shift in the demand curve to the right
questionBank.exp: Any price higher than equilibrium leads suppliers to bring more to market than people are willing to buy — a surplus.

questionBank.q: A customer opens a fixed deposit account, placing funds with the bank for a period of time. Which side of the financial market does this represent?
opts: The demand side, since the customer is providing funds
The supply side, since the customer is providing funds
The supply side, since the customer is borrowing funds
The demand side, since the customer is borrowing funds
questionBank.exp: Those who save or invest money, whether individuals or businesses, are on the supply side of the financial market.

questionBank.q: A small business takes out a loan to expand its operations. Which side of the financial market does this represent?
opts: The supply side, since the business is borrowing funds
The demand side, since the business is borrowing funds
The demand side, since the business is saving funds
The supply side, since the business is saving funds
questionBank.exp: Those who borrow money are on the demand side of the financial market.

questionBank.q: Which factor affecting demand is described as having a direct, immediate impact captured by the demand curve itself?
opts: Overall consumer income levels
The product's own price
Broader population demographics
Consumer tastes and preferences
questionBank.exp: A change in the price of a product directly impacts quantity demanded — the relationship the demand curve itself plots.

questionBank.q: As customers' incomes rise, a bank observes increased demand for premium current accounts. What type of good does this illustrate?
opts: An inferior good
A normal good
A structural good
An elastic good
questionBank.exp: For normal goods, demand tends to increase as consumer income increases.

questionBank.q: As customers' incomes rise, demand for a basic no-frills savings account declines as customers switch to premium products. What type of good does this illustrate?
opts: A normal good
An inferior good
A structural good
An elastic good
questionBank.exp: For inferior goods, demand may decrease as consumer income increases.

questionBank.q: A sudden consumer shift toward organic food products increases their demand at every price level. What factor caused this demand shift?
opts: A change in consumer income
A change in tastes and preferences
A change in population size
A change in production costs
questionBank.exp: Changes in consumer preferences or trends can shift demand, as with the manual's own organic-food example.

questionBank.q: A rapidly growing urban population leads to higher demand for rental housing across a city. What factor is driving this demand shift?
opts: A change in consumer tastes
Population and demographic growth
A change in production technology
A change in government subsidies
questionBank.exp: An increase in population can influence demand patterns, meaning more people demanding certain goods and services.

questionBank.q: Rising costs of imported raw materials force a manufacturer to reduce output at every price level. What factor is driving this supply shift?
opts: An increase in consumer income
An increase in production costs
An increase in population size
An increase in consumer tastes
questionBank.exp: Higher production costs, including materials, can reduce supply.

questionBank.q: A farm adopts new irrigation technology, allowing it to produce more crops at the same cost. What factor is driving this supply shift?
opts: A change in consumer tastes
An advance in production technology
A change in population demographics
A change in government taxation
questionBank.exp: Advances in technology can lead to more efficient production processes, increasing supply.

questionBank.q: A government introduces subsidies for fertilizer purchases, and farmers subsequently increase the quantity of crops they bring to market. What factor explains this supply shift?
opts: A rise in consumer income levels
A government subsidy reducing production costs
A shift in consumer tastes and preferences
A rise in the general population
questionBank.exp: Government subsidies to farmers, as the manual notes, can increase the supply of agricultural products.

questionBank.q: A severe drought destroys a large share of a region's wheat crop before harvest. What effect does this have on the supply curve?
opts: Supply increases as availability improves
Supply decreases as availability is disrupted
Demand decreases as tastes shift away from wheat
Demand increases as population grows
questionBank.exp: Events like droughts can disrupt supply chains and reduce the availability of certain goods.

questionBank.q: If demand for a good increases while supply also increases at the same time, what happens to equilibrium quantity?
opts: Equilibrium quantity decreases
Equilibrium quantity increases
Equilibrium quantity stays exactly the same
Equilibrium price decreases while quantity falls
questionBank.exp: A simultaneous increase in both demand and supply increases equilibrium quantity.

questionBank.q: A rise in the price of rice alone causes buyers to purchase less rice, without any other factor changing. How is this represented on a demand diagram?
opts: A shift of the entire demand curve to the left
A movement along the existing demand curve
A shift of the entire demand curve to the right
A movement along the existing supply curve
questionBank.exp: A price change for the good itself causes movement along the existing demand curve, not a shift of the curve.

questionBank.q: A new government subsidy lowers farmers' production costs at every possible price. How is this represented on a supply diagram?
opts: A movement along the existing supply curve
A shift of the entire supply curve to the right
A shift of the entire supply curve to the left
A movement along the existing demand curve
questionBank.exp: A non-price factor like a subsidy shifts the entire supply curve, here to the right since more is supplied at every price.

questionBank.q: A demand schedule shows that at ₦20 per unit, 150 units are demanded, and at ₦10 per unit, 300 units are demanded. What does this data confirm?
opts: A direct relationship between price and quantity demanded
An inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded
No relationship between price and quantity demanded
A relationship that reverses above ₦20 per unit
questionBank.exp: As price falls from ₦20 to ₦10, quantity demanded rises from 150 to 300 — confirming the inverse relationship of the Law of Demand.

questionBank.q: If production costs rise sharply for a good while demand stays unchanged, what happens to the market equilibrium?
opts: Equilibrium price falls and equilibrium quantity rises
Equilibrium price rises and equilibrium quantity falls
Equilibrium price rises and equilibrium quantity also rises
Equilibrium price and quantity remain exactly unchanged
questionBank.exp: Higher production costs reduce supply, shifting the supply curve left, which raises equilibrium price and lowers equilibrium quantity.

questionBank.q: If population grows while the supply curve for housing remains unchanged, what happens to the market equilibrium?
opts: Equilibrium price falls and equilibrium quantity falls
Equilibrium price rises and equilibrium quantity rises
Equilibrium price rises and equilibrium quantity falls
Equilibrium price and quantity remain exactly unchanged
questionBank.exp: Population growth increases demand, shifting the demand curve right; with supply unchanged, both equilibrium price and quantity rise.

questionBank.q: A bank notices that a rise in its lending rate barely reduces the volume of loans customers request. How should the bank interpret this pattern?
opts: Demand for its loans is relatively elastic
Demand for its loans is relatively inelastic
Supply of its loans is relatively inelastic
Supply of its loans is relatively elastic
questionBank.exp: When price changes cause only minor changes in quantity, demand is inelastic — the same concept applied to loan demand rather than eggs.

questionBank.q: A nationwide increase in average household income leads more customers to apply for car loans at Access Bank, even though lending rates have not changed. Per the course material's distinction, this is best described as:
opts: A movement along the existing demand curve, caused by the unchanged interest rate
A movement along the supply curve, caused by a change in production costs
A shift in the demand curve, caused by a non-price factor (rising consumer income)
Market equilibrium being re-established at a lower price
questionBank.exp: A non-price factor such as rising income shifts the entire demand curve rather than moving along it.

questionBank.q: A rise in the cost of imported diesel used to power factory generators leads a Nigerian manufacturer to supply fewer units of its product at every price level. Per the course material, this is an example of which supply factor?
opts: Technology and innovation
Government policy
Production costs
Weather and natural disasters
questionBank.exp: The course lists production costs (labour, materials, energy) as a key factor affecting supply.

questionBank.q: A textile firm installs automated weaving machines, allowing it to supply significantly more fabric at the same price as before. Per the course material, this increase in supply is driven by which factor?
opts: Technology and innovation improving production efficiency
Production costs rising
Government policy restricting imports
A shift in consumer tastes and preferences
questionBank.exp: The course lists technology and innovation as a factor that increases supply through more efficient production.

questionBank.q: A government subsidy programme for fertiliser leads Nigerian farmers to increase the quantity of maize they are willing to supply at every price level. Per the course material, this illustrates which supply factor?
opts: Weather and natural disasters
Government policies, such as subsidies, affecting supply
A shift in consumer income
A change in population and demographics
questionBank.exp: The course cites subsidies as a government policy that can increase agricultural supply.

questionBank.q: The course material instructs facilitators to explain why market equilibrium, though a useful theoretical concept, is rarely if ever attained in the real world. The best explanation consistent with this instruction is that:
opts: Government price controls make equilibrium illegal in most markets
Equilibrium can only exist in markets with a single buyer and a single seller
Equilibrium is a mathematical concept with no relevance to real-world pricing
The conditions affecting supply and demand are constantly changing, so the market never settles at a single resting point
questionBank.exp: Continuously changing conditions (new information, shifting tastes, policy changes) keep real markets from settling permanently at one equilibrium point.

questionBank.q: When the price of eggs drops from N25 to N10 per dozen and weekly demand rises from 200 to 400 crates, the course concludes demand is elastic. Which mathematical logic BEST supports this conclusion?
opts: Price fell by 60%, quantity rose by 100% — since |%ΔQ| > |%ΔP|, demand is elastic
Price fell by N15, quantity rose by 200 — absolute changes show elastic demand
Price fell below the equilibrium, triggering a shortage
Revenue stayed constant, confirming unit elasticity
questionBank.exp: Elasticity = %ΔQ / %ΔP. Price fell from N25 to N10 = 60% drop; quantity rose from 200 to 400 = 100% rise. Since 100% > 60%, the responsiveness of quantity exceeds the price change, confirming elastic demand.

questionBank.q: The course states that fuel and cigarettes are examples of inelastic demand. What is the PRIMARY economic reason for this inelasticity?
opts: Fuel and cigarettes have no substitutes, and cigarettes are addictive — buyers are insensitive to price
Their prices are controlled by the government, making demand appear unresponsive
Both goods are luxury items with high income elasticity
Producers have monopoly power that prevents price signals from affecting quantity demanded
questionBank.exp: Inelastic demand arises when consumers are minimally responsive to price changes. For fuel (few substitutes, necessity) and cigarettes (addictive), quantity purchased changes little even with significant price movements — lack of substitutes and addiction are the core reasons.

questionBank.q: In the course's egg market example, at N33/dozen the market clears at 300 crates/week. If the CBN policy suddenly increases disposable income for middle-income earners, which shift occurs and what is the EXPECTED effect on equilibrium?
opts: Supply curve shifts right; price falls, quantity rises
Demand curve shifts right; price rises above N33, quantity rises above 300
Supply curve shifts left; price rises, quantity falls
Demand curve shifts left; price falls below N33, quantity falls below 300
questionBank.exp: Higher disposable income increases purchasing power (a demand-side factor). The demand curve shifts RIGHT (more demanded at every price), moving equilibrium to a higher price and higher quantity than the original N33/300 crates equilibrium.

questionBank.q: The course notes that savers and investors are on the supply side, while borrowers are on the demand side of the financial market. If the MPR is cut from 27% to 20%, what supply-demand dynamic occurs in the credit market?
opts: Supply of credit contracts as banks earn less on deposits; demand for loans falls
Supply of credit expands (banks lend more cheaply); demand for loans increases — equilibrium loan quantity rises
Demand for loans falls because cheaper loans reduce the incentive to borrow wisely
Supply of credit falls and demand stays constant, creating a credit shortage
questionBank.exp: A lower MPR reduces the cost of funds for banks (supply side), enabling them to offer cheaper loans — shifting the credit supply curve right. Simultaneously, lower interest rates make borrowing cheaper, shifting the demand for credit right. Both forces increase equilibrium loan volume.

questionBank.q: A severe drought destroys 40% of Nigeria's tomato harvest. Using the framework from Module 3, identify the correct supply-demand outcome:
opts: Weather shocks affect demand, not supply; price is unaffected
Supply shifts left (weather/natural disaster factor); equilibrium price rises and quantity falls, creating a temporary shortage at the old price
Supply shifts right because farmers work harder after the drought; price falls
Demand shifts right because consumers want tomatoes more after the drought
questionBank.exp: The course lists weather and natural disasters as factors affecting SUPPLY. A drought reduces supply (left shift), raising equilibrium price and reducing equilibrium quantity. At the old price, a shortage emerges until price adjusts upward.

questionBank.q: At price P1 (above equilibrium N33), sellers bring 500 crates while buyers only want 150 crates. This situation is called a _____ and will cause price to move _____.
opts: Shortage; upward toward equilibrium
Surplus; downward toward equilibrium
Surplus; upward until supply is exhausted
Shortage; downward because sellers panic
questionBank.exp: When price exceeds equilibrium, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded — this is a SURPLUS (excess supply). Competitive pressure from unsold stock forces sellers to lower prices, driving the market back toward equilibrium.

questionBank.q: The government subsidises poultry farmers, reducing their production costs. Simultaneously, a new dietary trend makes eggs less popular. What is the NET effect on egg market equilibrium?
opts: Price definitely rises; quantity effect is ambiguous
Price effect is ambiguous; quantity definitely rises
Price definitely falls; quantity effect is ambiguous
Both price and quantity definitely rise
questionBank.exp: Subsidy → supply shifts right (price falls, quantity rises). Demand shift left from dietary trend (price falls, quantity falls). Price falls from BOTH effects (certain). Quantity change is ambiguous — supply increase pushes it up while demand decrease pushes it down.

questionBank.q: A new technology allows Nigerian poultry farmers to produce eggs at 40% lower cost per crate. Simultaneously, the Eid al-Fitr celebration season dramatically increases consumer demand for eggs. What is the CERTAIN outcome at market equilibrium?
opts: Price rises; quantity change is ambiguous
Quantity supplied increases; price change is ambiguous
Quantity rises (certain); price effect is ambiguous (supply pushes price down, demand pushes it up)
Both price and quantity fall
questionBank.exp: Technology lowers production costs → supply shifts RIGHT (more at every price → downward price pressure, upward quantity). Eid demand surge → demand shifts RIGHT (more demanded at every price → upward price pressure, upward quantity). Quantity rises from BOTH shifts (certain). Price: supply pulls it down, demand pushes it up — net effect is ambiguous.

questionBank.q: A sudden consumer preference for healthier eating habits increases demand for organic produce in Lagos markets, even though prices have not changed. Per the course material, this demand change is driven by:
opts: A change in price, causing a movement along the demand curve
A change in production costs, causing a shift in the supply curve
A change in tastes and preferences, causing a shift in the demand curve
A change in population size, causing structural scarcity
questionBank.exp: The course's own example links a shift toward healthier preferences with a shift in the demand curve for organic products.

questionBank.q: A prolonged drought in northern Nigeria disrupts irrigation and reduces the quantity of tomatoes farmers can supply at every price level. Per the course material, this illustrates which supply factor?
opts: Technology and innovation
Production costs alone, unrelated to weather
Weather and natural disasters disrupting supply chains
A shift in consumer tastes toward alternative vegetables
questionBank.exp: The course lists weather and natural disasters as events that can disrupt supply chains and reduce availability.

questionBank.q: Environments where buyers and sellers interact to exchange goods and services, determining how resources are allocated and prices set, are best described as what?
opts: Economic policies
Economic markets
Economic cycles
Economic indicators
questionBank.exp: Economic markets are defined as environments where buyers and sellers interact to exchange goods and services, dictating resource allocation and price determination.

questionBank.q: Why is understanding different market structures considered crucial for businesses and policymakers?
opts: It informs decisions on office interior design choices
It informs decisions on production, pricing, and resource allocation
It informs decisions on employee vacation scheduling
It informs decisions on company logo redesigns
questionBank.exp: Understanding economic markets helps in making informed decisions about production, pricing, and resource allocation.

questionBank.q: Which characteristic distinguishes perfect competition in terms of market participants?
opts: A small number of buyers and sellers, each able to influence price
A large number of buyers and sellers, none able to influence price
A single seller controlling the entire market
A few dominant firms controlling most of the market
questionBank.exp: In perfect competition there are numerous buyers and sellers, none of whom have the power to influence the market price.

questionBank.q: In perfect competition, products offered by different sellers are typically what?
opts: Differentiated, making suppliers easily distinguishable to consumers
Homogeneous, making suppliers indistinguishable to consumers
Branded, making suppliers command premium loyalty
Regulated, making suppliers follow identical safety standards
questionBank.exp: All products in perfect competition are identical, making it impossible for consumers to differentiate between suppliers.

questionBank.q: Perfect competition assumes that both buyers and sellers have access to what?
opts: Complete control over the government's monetary policy
Complete knowledge of prices, quality, and availability
Complete ownership of the industry's production facilities
Complete exemption from industry safety regulations
questionBank.exp: Perfect information means both buyers and sellers have complete knowledge of the market, including prices, quality, and availability.

questionBank.q: How easily can firms enter or leave a perfectly competitive market?
opts: With difficulty, due to high capital requirements
Easily, without incurring significant costs
With difficulty, due to strict government licensing
Easily, but only with regulator approval each time
questionBank.exp: Firms can easily enter or exit a perfectly competitive market without incurring significant costs.

questionBank.q: Why are individual firms in perfect competition described as 'price takers'?
opts: They can set prices above the market rate
They must accept the prevailing market price
They can set prices below production cost
They negotiate prices individually with each buyer
questionBank.exp: Individual firms have no influence on the market price and must accept the prevailing price — hence 'price takers'.

questionBank.q: A well-developed securities market with free-flowing information and numerous participants is cited as an example of which market structure?
opts: Monopolistic competition
Perfect competition
An oligopoly
A monopoly
questionBank.exp: The manual cites the well-developed stock market, with its free flow of information, as an example of perfect competition.

questionBank.q: Which is identified as an advantage of a perfectly competitive market?
opts: A single firm can set prices without consequence
Resources are allocated in the most efficient manner
Entry barriers protect existing firms from new competitors
Consumers have limited access to pricing information
questionBank.exp: A stated advantage of perfect competition is that resources are allocated in the most efficient manner, aided by shared knowledge and no entry barriers.

questionBank.q: Monopolistic competition is characterized by many sellers offering products that are how?
opts: Completely identical to one another across all sellers
Slightly different from one another, creating brand differentiation
Controlled entirely by a single dominant producer
Restricted by government-set production quotas
questionBank.exp: In monopolistic competition, firms produce goods or services slightly different from competitors, leading to brand differentiation.

questionBank.q: Why do firms in monopolistic competition have some control over the price they charge?
opts: Government regulation fixes minimum prices for all sellers
Brand loyalty and perceived quality differences reduce direct price comparison
A single firm owns all production facilities in the market
Import tariffs eliminate price competition from other sellers
questionBank.exp: Firms have some degree of price control due to brand loyalty and perceived differences in quality.

questionBank.q: Different restaurants offering distinct menus, atmospheres, and dining experiences to attract customers exemplify which market structure?
opts: Perfect competition
Monopolistic competition
An oligopoly
A monopoly
questionBank.exp: The restaurant industry is the manual's own example of monopolistic competition, given its product/experience differentiation.

questionBank.q: Why does 'monopolistic competition' carry that particular name?
opts: It combines features of both fiscal and monetary policy
It combines features of both monopoly and perfect competition
It combines features of both supply and demand curves
It combines features of both domestic and foreign trade
questionBank.exp: The name derives from combining features of a monopoly with features of perfect competition.

questionBank.q: What is a recognized disadvantage of monopolistic competition, alongside its benefits of differentiation and innovation?
opts: It can lead to a single firm controlling the entire supply
It can lead to higher prices and inefficient production
It can lead to complete elimination of consumer choice
It can lead to fixed prices set by government decree
questionBank.exp: While it fosters differentiation and innovation, monopolistic competition can also result in higher prices, inefficient production, and reduced competition.

questionBank.q: An oligopoly is a market structure defined primarily by what characteristic?
opts: A large number of small firms with no individual market power
A small number of dominant firms holding significant market power
A single firm holding complete control of the market
Countless firms selling an identical, unbranded product
questionBank.exp: An oligopoly is defined by a small number of firms dominating the market, resulting in significant market power.

questionBank.q: In an oligopoly, why does the pricing decision of one firm typically affect its rivals directly?
opts: Firms are legally required to match each other's prices
Firms are interdependent, so each decision impacts others' market share
Firms share a single production facility across the industry
Firms are owned by the same parent holding company
questionBank.exp: Interdependence means the decisions of one oligopoly firm directly impact the market share and profits of other firms in the industry.

questionBank.q: Why is it typically difficult for new firms to enter an oligopolistic market?
opts: Government bans any new entrants by law
High capital requirements and other significant barriers exist
Existing firms hold exclusive patents on every product feature
Consumers refuse to purchase from any new brand
questionBank.exp: Entry into an oligopoly is difficult due to high capital requirements or other significant barriers.

questionBank.q: The dominance of a small number of major companies in Nigeria's mobile network industry is best described as an example of which market structure?
opts: Perfect competition
An oligopoly
Monopolistic competition
A monopoly
questionBank.exp: The manual cites Mobile Network Operators in Nigeria, alongside the automobile industry, as examples of oligopoly.

questionBank.q: Which is cited as a potential advantage of an oligopoly for consumers?
opts: Unlimited firms make it easier to compare products
A limited number of firms makes it easier to compare products
A single firm eliminates the need to compare products
Government price controls remove the need to compare products
questionBank.exp: A limited number of oligopoly firms makes it easier for customers to compare and choose products, per the manual's listed advantages.

questionBank.q: A monopoly is a market structure in which how many suppliers exist?
opts: Countless suppliers, none able to influence price individually
A single supplier controlling all supply and pricing
A few dominant suppliers, each holding partial market power
Many suppliers, each offering a slightly different product
questionBank.exp: A monopoly has a single seller, giving them complete control over supply and pricing.

questionBank.q: Why can a monopolist maintain its market position so effectively?
opts: It offers a product identical to all of its competitors
It offers a product with no close substitutes
It offers a product regulated at a fixed minimum price
It offers a product priced below its competitors' costs
questionBank.exp: The monopolist offers a unique product with no close substitutes, giving them a virtual monopoly on that good or service.

questionBank.q: Complete market power in a monopoly allows the seller to do what, without fear of competition?
opts: Set prices but never adjust production quantities
Set both prices and quantities independently
Set quantities but never adjust prices
Set neither prices nor quantities without regulator approval
questionBank.exp: A monopolist can set both prices and quantities without fear of competition, due to complete market power.

questionBank.q: Nigeria's railway system, operated exclusively by the Federal Government in most of the country, is cited as an example of which market structure?
opts: An oligopoly
A monopoly
Perfect competition
Monopolistic competition
questionBank.exp: The manual cites Nigeria's railways, run exclusively by the Federal Government, as an example of monopoly, alongside utilities like water and electricity.

questionBank.q: Traditionally, who benefits most directly from a monopoly's market position, and who bears the corresponding cost?
opts: Consumers benefit; the monopolist bears reduced overall profit
The monopolist benefits; consumers bear higher prices
Competitors benefit; the monopolist bears reduced market share
Regulators benefit; consumers bear increased tax obligations
questionBank.exp: Monopolies traditionally benefit the companies that have them, while harming consumer interests due to a lack of competition.

questionBank.q: Comparing efficiency across market structures, which is generally considered the most efficient, and which the least?
opts: Monopoly is most efficient; perfect competition is least efficient
Perfect competition is most efficient; monopoly is least efficient
Oligopoly is most efficient; monopolistic competition is least efficient
All market structures are considered equally efficient
questionBank.exp: Perfect competition is considered the most efficient market structure, while monopoly is least efficient due to lack of competition.

questionBank.q: How does price determination differ between perfect competition and monopoly?
opts: The government sets price in perfect competition; the market sets price under monopoly
Market forces set price in perfect competition; the monopolist sets price
Consumers vote on price in perfect competition; suppliers vote under monopoly
Prices are fixed by law under both perfect competition and monopoly
questionBank.exp: Prices are determined by market forces in perfect competition, while monopolies have the power to set prices themselves.

questionBank.q: Which market structures are most associated with encouraging firms to differentiate and innovate their products?
opts: Perfect competition and monopoly
Monopolistic competition and oligopoly
Perfect competition and oligopoly
Monopoly and monopolistic competition
questionBank.exp: Monopolistic competition and oligopoly encourage firms to differentiate and innovate, while perfect competition may lead to less innovation.

questionBank.q: Which market structure is generally associated with the highest level of consumer welfare, due to lower prices and greater choice?
opts: A monopoly
Perfect competition
An oligopoly
Monopolistic competition
questionBank.exp: Perfect competition generally leads to higher consumer welfare due to lower prices and greater choice.

questionBank.q: A bank is assessing a loan applicant that operates as a dominant, low-competition firm within its industry. How does this market position typically affect the bank's risk assessment?
opts: It suggests greater exposure to unpredictable price wars
It suggests greater stability of profit and cash flow
It suggests weaker bargaining power with suppliers
It suggests higher vulnerability to new market entrants
questionBank.exp: A customer's market strength determines the stability of its profit and cash flow — a firm with greater market strength is less affected by economic developments.

questionBank.q: A bank's loan applicant is one of only a handful of firms in its industry, and its pricing decisions consistently trigger matching responses from its closest rivals. Which market structure does this business most likely operate in?
opts: Perfect competition
An oligopoly
Monopolistic competition
A monopoly
questionBank.exp: A small number of dominant, interdependent firms whose decisions affect rivals' market share is the defining signature of an oligopoly.

questionBank.q: Which two characteristics, per the course material, distinguish a perfectly competitive market?
opts: Differentiated products and high barriers to entry
Few dominant firms and significant market power
Homogeneous products and complete (perfect) information available to buyers and sellers
A single seller and a unique product with no substitutes
questionBank.exp: The course lists homogeneous products and perfect information among the defining characteristics of perfect competition.

questionBank.q: Per the course material's characteristics, monopolistic competition features firms that:
opts: Sell identical products and have no influence over price at all
Offer differentiated products and have some degree of control over price due to brand loyalty
Are the sole supplier in the market with complete pricing power
Face extremely high barriers preventing new firms from entering
questionBank.exp: Monopolistic competition is defined by differentiated products and some pricing power from brand loyalty, with easy entry.

questionBank.q: The course material explains that the term 'monopolistic competition' derives its name from the fact that this market structure:
opts: Is identical in every respect to a pure monopoly
Refers to a market with only government-owned firms
Combines features of a monopoly (some pricing power) with features of perfect competition (many sellers, easy entry)
Describes firms that have successfully eliminated all competitors
questionBank.exp: The course explicitly states the name reflects a combination of monopoly and perfect-competition features.

questionBank.q: Per the course material, a potential disadvantage of monopolistic competition is that it can result in:
opts: Complete elimination of consumer choice
Higher prices and inefficient production compared to perfect competition
A single firm controlling the entire market
Zero product differentiation among competing firms
questionBank.exp: The course lists higher prices and inefficient production as potential disadvantages of monopolistic competition.

questionBank.q: Per the course material, oligopolistic markets are characterised by high barriers to entry and products that:
opts: Must always be perfectly homogeneous, with no differentiation permitted
Cannot be compared across the few dominant firms
May be either homogeneous or differentiated, depending on the industry
Are always unique with no close substitutes anywhere in the market
questionBank.exp: The course notes oligopoly products may be homogeneous or differentiated, depending on the specific industry.

questionBank.q: Per the course material's characteristics of monopoly, the monopolist is described as being able to:
opts: Set prices and quantities without fear of competition, due to complete market power
Influence price only marginally, since several close competitors constrain its pricing
Enter and exit the market freely, since barriers to entry are minimal
Offer a product with many close substitutes available from rival firms
questionBank.exp: The course defines monopoly as having complete market power to set prices and quantities without competitive pressure.

questionBank.q: Per the course material, the Nigerian Railway Corporation is cited as an example of monopoly because rail transport on federal lines is exclusive to the Federal Government, although the course material also notes a nuance regarding:
opts: The complete absence of any rail transport anywhere in Nigeria
The privatisation of all federal railway assets to private investors
The Railway Corporation's adoption of perfect-competition pricing
Lagos State's introduction of its own light railway system
questionBank.exp: The course notes that while federal rail is a monopoly, Lagos State has since introduced its own light railway system.

questionBank.q: Per the course material's comparative analysis, which market structure is considered the most efficient, and which the least efficient, respectively?
opts: Monopoly is most efficient; perfect competition is least efficient
Oligopoly is most efficient; monopolistic competition is least efficient
All four market structures are equally efficient under the course's framework
Perfect competition is most efficient; monopoly is least efficient, due to lack of competition
questionBank.exp: The course's comparative analysis ranks perfect competition as most efficient and monopoly as least efficient.

questionBank.q: Per the course material's comparative analysis, prices in perfect competition are determined by market forces, while in monopoly, prices are:
opts: Also determined entirely by market forces, with no firm-level influence
Set by the government exclusively, with the monopolist having no input
Within the monopolist's power to set, given its complete market control
Identical to the prices that would prevail under perfect competition
questionBank.exp: The course's comparative analysis notes monopolies have the power to set prices, unlike perfectly competitive firms.

questionBank.q: Per the course material's comparative analysis, which market structures are described as encouraging firms to differentiate and innovate?
opts: Perfect competition and monopoly
Monopolistic competition and oligopoly
Only perfect competition
Only monopoly
questionBank.exp: The course's comparative analysis attributes greater innovation and differentiation to monopolistic competition and oligopoly.

questionBank.q: A well-developed stock exchange is cited in the course as an example of near-perfect competition. Which characteristic of perfect competition does a stock exchange MOST closely embody that physical goods markets often fail?
opts: Large number of identical products
Perfect information — free flow of price and trading data
Zero barriers to entry for any trader
Homogeneous products — all shares are identical
questionBank.exp: The course specifically highlights 'free flow of information' as the reason the stock market is cited as a near-perfect competition example. Price discovery and trade data are publicly and instantly available, unlike most physical goods markets.

questionBank.q: Nigeria's mobile network operators (MTN, Airtel, Glo, 9Mobile) are cited as examples of oligopoly. A new entrant wants to compete. What is the PRIMARY structural barrier they face?
opts: All products are homogeneous, so brand loyalty is impossible
High capital requirements for spectrum licenses and infrastructure make entry prohibitively costly
Perfect information means the new entrant can easily replicate incumbent strategies
