Statutory transfers
questionBank.exp: Capital expenditure, at ₦21.21 trillion (36.3% of the pie chart), is the largest single expenditure category.

questionBank.q: According to the Nigeria 2026 budget breakdown, approximately how much is allocated to debt servicing?
opts: ₦4.1 trillion
₦15.91 trillion
₦21.21 trillion
₦15.25 trillion
questionBank.exp: Debt servicing is allocated ₦15.91 trillion in the Nigeria 2026 budget.

questionBank.q: In the Nigeria 2026 budget's key sectoral allocations, which sector receives the largest share, according to the chart?
opts: Infrastructure
Defence-and-security
Education
Health
questionBank.exp: Defence and Security receives the largest sectoral share, at 36.1%, per the sectoral allocation chart.

questionBank.q: Given that the Nigeria 2026 budget carries a large deficit of roughly ₦25.27 trillion alongside heavy capital expenditure, what does this fiscal stance most closely resemble?
opts: A contractionary fiscal stance geared toward reducing inflation
An expansionary fiscal stance geared toward stimulating growth
A balanced fiscal stance with revenue matching expenditure
A neutral fiscal stance with no effect on economic output
questionBank.exp: High deficit spending with heavy capital investment reflects an expansionary stance — increased expenditure aimed at growth, at the cost of a larger deficit.

questionBank.q: Why should bankers stay conversant with their country's annual budget, according to the material?
opts: To gauge the direction of global oil prices
To gauge the direction the country is headed
To gauge the direction of a competitor bank's strategy
To gauge the direction of the stock exchange index
questionBank.exp: Bankers should be conversant with the national budget to gauge the direction the country is headed in the budget year.

questionBank.q: How can a banker use knowledge of the national budget to benefit their institution directly?
opts: By identifying opportunities to avoid regulatory compliance
By identifying business opportunities arising from the budget
By identifying opportunities to reduce staff headcount
By identifying opportunities to relocate branch offices
questionBank.exp: Bankers should study the budget to find business opportunities it presents for the bank.

questionBank.q: A customer asks their relationship manager how the new budget might affect their business. Why is the banker expected to be able to respond?
opts: To provide legal representation in budget-related disputes
To provide advisory services grounded in the year's budget
To provide tax filing services on the customer's behalf
To provide audit services unrelated to the national budget
questionBank.exp: Bankers should be able to provide advisory services to customers or answer their questions on the year's budget.

questionBank.q: Monetary policy refers to actions taken by a country's central bank to manage which two things?
opts: Government spending and taxation
The money supply and interest rates
Import tariffs and export subsidies
Stock prices and bond yields
questionBank.exp: Monetary policy is the set of actions taken by a central bank to control and manage the money supply and interest rates.

questionBank.q: The primary goal of monetary policy is achieved mainly by controlling what?
opts: The volume of government spending
The volume of money in circulation
The volume of imported goods
The volume of company profits
questionBank.exp: Monetary policy's objectives are achieved by controlling the volume of money in circulation, i.e. money supply.

questionBank.q: M1, the narrow measure of money supply, is also referred to as what?
opts: Quasi money
Transaction money
Broad money
Reserve money
questionBank.exp: M1 is also called transaction money, as it is available to settle transactions immediately.

questionBank.q: M1 is composed of which two elements?
opts: Savings account balances, and time deposit balances
Notes and coins in circulation, and demand deposit balances
Notes and coins in circulation, and time deposit balances
Demand deposit balances, and treasury bill holdings
questionBank.exp: M1 comprises notes and coins in circulation, and balances on demand deposit accounts.

questionBank.q: M2, the broad measure of money supply, is also referred to as what?
opts: Transaction money
Quasi money
Narrow money
Reserve money
questionBank.exp: M2 is also called quasi money, the broad measure of money supply.

questionBank.q: M2 includes M1 plus which additional balances?
opts: Foreign currency reserve balances
Savings and time deposit balances
Government treasury bill balances
Corporate bond holding balances
questionBank.exp: M2 adds balances on savings accounts and time deposit accounts to M1's components.

questionBank.q: A customer's funds sitting in a fixed-term time deposit account would be captured under which measure of money supply?
opts: M1, since time deposits are part of the narrow measure
M2, since time deposits are part of the broad measure
Neither M1 nor M2, since time deposits are excluded
Both M1 and M2 equally, since the split does not apply
questionBank.exp: Time deposit balances are explicitly part of M2, the broad or quasi measure of money supply.

questionBank.q: Central banks generally control money supply using which four tools?
opts: Tax rates, government spending, borrowing, and subsidies
Reserve requirements, MPR, open market operations, and liquidity ratio
Import quotas, export subsidies, tariffs, and trade agreements
Wage controls, price ceilings, rent controls, and rationing
questionBank.exp: The four tools of monetary policy are reserve requirements, the rediscount rate (MPR), open market operations, and liquidity requirements.

questionBank.q: Nigeria's Cash Reserve Ratio for deposit money banks currently stands at approximately what level?
questionBank.exp: Nigeria's CRR is stated as 45% for deposit money banks (DMBs), and 16% for merchant banks.

questionBank.q: If a central bank raises the reserve requirement, what is the expected effect on money in circulation?
opts: Money in circulation increases, since more must be held in reserve
Money in circulation decreases, since more must be held in reserve
Money in circulation stays fixed, since reserves are unrelated
Money in circulation decreases, because export revenues fall sharply
questionBank.exp: Increasing the reserve requirement reduces the volume of money in circulation since more money must be held in reserve rather than lent out.

questionBank.q: The Monetary Policy Rate in Nigeria, the rate at which the Central Bank lends to commercial banks, currently stands at approximately what level?
questionBank.exp: Nigeria's MPR is stated as 27.0%.

questionBank.q: When the Central Bank lowers the MPR, what is the expected effect on borrowing by businesses and individuals?
opts: Borrowing becomes more expensive, discouraging borrowing
Borrowing becomes cheaper, encouraging more borrowing
Borrowing costs stay the same, since MPR is unrelated to lending rates
Borrowing becomes cheaper, but businesses stop borrowing regardless
questionBank.exp: When the government wants to stimulate activity, the Central Bank may lower MPR, making it cheaper for businesses and individuals to borrow.

questionBank.q: When a central bank buys government securities on the open market, what is the expected effect on the money supply?
opts: The money supply decreases, as money is injected into the banking system
The money supply increases, as money is injected into the banking system
The money supply increases, as money is withdrawn from the banking system
The money supply stays constant, since securities trades don't affect money
questionBank.exp: When the Central Bank buys securities, it results in an injection of money into the banking system, increasing the money supply.

questionBank.q: A central bank sells a large volume of treasury bills to commercial banks. What effect does this open market operation have?
opts: It injects money into the banking system, increasing the money supply
It removes money from the banking system, reducing the money supply
It has no effect on the money supply, only on interest rates
It removes money from circulation, but increases the money supply
questionBank.exp: Selling securities removes money from the banking system, reducing the money supply.

questionBank.q: Nigeria's Liquidity Ratio, the share of deposits banks must hold in liquid and semi-liquid instruments, currently stands at approximately what level?
questionBank.exp: Nigeria's Liquidity Ratio is stated as 30%.

questionBank.q: If a central bank raises the liquidity requirement, what is the expected effect on funds available for banks to lend?
opts: Available lending funds increase, since more must be held in liquid instruments
Available lending funds decrease, since more must be held in liquid instruments
Available lending funds stay fixed, since liquidity is unrelated to lending
Available lending funds decrease, because export earnings decline sharply
questionBank.exp: Raising the liquidity requirement reduces the funds available to banks for disbursement, reducing the money supply.

questionBank.q: Under an expansionary monetary policy stance, how does a central bank typically adjust reserve requirements?
opts: It raises reserve requirements to expand the money supply
It reduces reserve requirements to expand the money supply
It reduces reserve requirements to contract the money supply
It leaves reserve requirements unchanged to expand the money supply
questionBank.exp: Under expansionary policy, reducing reserve requirements creates excess reserves and induces banks to extend more loans, expanding the money supply.

questionBank.q: Under a restrictive monetary policy stance, how does a central bank typically adjust the rediscount rate (MPR)?
opts: It lowers the MPR to discourage borrowing from the central bank
It raises the MPR to discourage borrowing from the central bank
It raises the MPR to encourage borrowing from the central bank
It leaves the MPR unchanged to discourage borrowing
questionBank.exp: Under restrictive policy, raising the rediscount rate discourages borrowing from the central bank, so banks extend fewer loans.

questionBank.q: A rise in the Monetary Policy Rate most directly affects which cost faced by borrowers?
opts: The cost of importing raw materials
The cost of borrowing and servicing loans
The cost of hiring new employees
The cost of leasing office space
questionBank.exp: The MPR directly regulates the cost of borrowing and the cost of servicing loans, per the six listed effects of the MPR on the economy.

questionBank.q: Through its effect on commercial lending rates, the MPR most directly regulates what in the economy?
opts: The availability of imported goods
The availability of credit
The availability of skilled labor
The availability of foreign tourists
questionBank.exp: The MPR is listed as regulating the availability of credit in the economy.

questionBank.q: Because the MPR affects borrowing costs for businesses, it indirectly regulates which broader economic outcome?
opts: The level of rainfall
The level of employment
The level of literacy
The level of internet penetration
questionBank.exp: The MPR is listed as regulating employment, since borrowing costs affect business activity and hiring.

questionBank.q: Facing high and rising inflation, which monetary policy action would the central bank most likely take to combat it?
opts: Lower interest rates to boost spending and demand
Raise interest rates to reduce spending
Raise government spending to boost demand
Lower taxes to boost consumer spending
questionBank.exp: To combat high inflation, the suggested monetary response is raising interest rates, making borrowing more expensive and reducing demand.

questionBank.q: Facing a weakening exchange rate, which fiscal policy action is suggested to support the currency over time?
opts: Increase domestic consumption through import subsidies
Promote exports through incentives and improved trade infrastructure
Raise interest rates to attract foreign reserves
Sell foreign currency reserves in the open market
questionBank.exp: The suggested fiscal response to poor exchange rates is promoting exports through incentives and improved trade infrastructure, strengthening the balance of payments.

questionBank.q: Following a VAT rate increase that raises the cost of living for lower-income households, which fiscal measure is suggested to soften the impact?
opts: A further increase in the VAT rate on essential goods
Targeted income support or subsidies for essential goods
A reduction in the central bank's interest rate
An increase in the Cash Reserve Ratio for banks
questionBank.exp: The suggested fiscal response is targeted income support or subsidies for essential goods to mitigate the impact on lower-income individuals.

questionBank.q: Nigeria's 2026 budget has total expenditure of N58.47 trillion against revenue of N33.19 trillion. What type of budget is this, and what is the deficit?
opts: Surplus budget; N25.28 trillion surplus
Balanced budget; revenue and expenditure are within 5%
Deficit budget; the deficit is N25.28 trillion
Deficit budget; the deficit is N58.47 trillion
questionBank.exp: A deficit budget has expenditure exceeding revenue. N58.47T - N33.19T = N25.28T deficit. This matches the 2026 budget's stated deficit.

questionBank.q: The Nigerian government wants to stimulate economic recovery after a recession. The appropriate fiscal policy stance is:
opts: Contractionary — reduce spending and raise taxes to cut the deficit
Neutral — maintain current spending and tax levels unchanged
Expansionary — increase spending and/or reduce taxes to inject demand into the economy
Monetary — lower the MPR and reduce the CRR simultaneously
questionBank.exp: Expansionary fiscal policy (increased spending and/or tax cuts) injects resources into the economy, stimulating demand during a recession.

questionBank.q: A government implements contractionary fiscal policy during high inflation. The expected immediate effect on the private sector is:
opts: Increased consumer spending due to reduced competition with government for resources
Reduced aggregate demand as higher taxes and lower government spending withdraw resources
Higher investment because interest rates automatically fall when government spends less
Currency depreciation because contractionary policy reduces confidence
questionBank.exp: Contractionary fiscal policy withdraws resources from the economy — higher taxes reduce disposable income; lower spending reduces business revenues — both decrease aggregate demand.

questionBank.q: The 2026 Nigerian budget's debt servicing cost is N15.91 trillion. A banker should be concerned about this because:
opts: High debt servicing means less government spending on productive infrastructure that could stimulate the economy
Debt servicing payments increase the money supply, causing inflation
High debt servicing means the government will raise taxes immediately
Debt servicing reduces the CBN's foreign exchange reserves
questionBank.exp: High debt servicing consumes a large share of revenue, leaving less for productive capital spending. This can crowd out investment and slow economic growth.

questionBank.q: The difference between 'capital expenditure' and 'recurrent expenditure' in Nigeria's budget is:
opts: Capital expenditure pays civil servant salaries; recurrent expenditure builds infrastructure
Capital expenditure represents investment in assets like roads and hospitals; recurrent expenditure covers ongoing operational costs like debt servicing
Capital expenditure is funded by taxes; recurrent expenditure is funded by borrowing
Capital expenditure always leads to a budget surplus; recurrent creates a deficit
questionBank.exp: Capital expenditure is investment spending (infrastructure, assets). Recurrent expenditure covers ongoing costs (salaries, debt servicing, operations).

questionBank.q: If the Nigerian government increases personal income tax rates significantly, the MOST DIRECT effect on Access Bank is:
opts: Access Bank's corporate tax bill increases
Reduced household disposable income, potentially lowering retail loan demand and deposit growth
The CBN automatically raises the MPR in response
Foreign investors withdraw capital from Nigeria
questionBank.exp: Higher personal taxes reduce disposable income. Less disposable income means lower consumer spending, reduced ability to save (deposits) and potentially less demand for consumer credit.

questionBank.q: Monetary policy is described as 'managing the flow of water in a garden hose.' If the CBN is trying to prevent the garden from flooding (overheating), it would:
opts: Open the nozzle wider by lowering the MPR
Add more water to the hose by printing more money
Close the nozzle by raising the MPR to restrict money flow
Remove the hose entirely by eliminating the banking system
questionBank.exp: Overheating (inflation) is addressed by closing the nozzle — raising the MPR to make borrowing more expensive, reducing money flow and aggregate demand.

questionBank.q: The CBN's Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) is currently 45% for commercial banks. This means that for every N100 a bank receives in deposits:
opts: N45 must be held in reserve at the CBN, limiting funds available for lending to N55
N45 can be lent out; N55 must be held in reserve
N45 is used for operations; N55 is profit
The bank must raise N45 from shareholders as additional capital
questionBank.exp: The CRR mandates that banks hold 45% of deposits as reserves at the CBN. Only N55 of every N100 deposited can be deployed as loans or investments.

questionBank.q: When the CBN conducts open market operations by BUYING government bonds from commercial banks, the effect is:
opts: Money is withdrawn from the banking system, reducing money supply
Government debt is reduced, decreasing the fiscal deficit
Money is injected into the banking system, increasing the money supply and potentially lowering interest rates
Banks are forced to increase their reserve ratios
questionBank.exp: When CBN buys securities, it pays cash to banks — injecting money into the system. This increases money supply and typically lowers interest rates.

questionBank.q: The current Liquidity Ratio requirement in Nigeria is 30%. This means banks must:
opts: Hold 30% of assets in cash only
Ensure that 30% of their deposits are held in liquid and semi‑liquid instruments
Lend 30% of deposits to the government
Maintain 30% of their equity as CRR at the CBN
questionBank.exp: The Liquidity Ratio (30%) requires banks to hold 30% of deposits in liquid and semi‑liquid instruments, ensuring they can meet withdrawal demands.

questionBank.q: M1 (narrow money) includes which of the following components?
opts: Savings accounts, time deposits, and foreign currency holdings
Notes and coins in circulation plus balances in demand deposit accounts
All bank deposits plus government treasury bills
Corporate bonds and equity investments held by banks
questionBank.exp: M1 (narrow money / transaction money) consists of notes and coins in circulation plus demand deposit account balances — immediately available for transactions.

questionBank.q: M2 (broad money) differs from M1 primarily because M2:
opts: Includes only cash and excludes all deposits
Includes M1 plus savings and time deposits, capturing less liquid forms of money
Excludes demand deposits and only includes long‑term savings
Is a measure of government debt outstanding
questionBank.exp: M2 = M1 + savings deposits + time deposits. It is broader, capturing quasi‑money — funds not immediately usable for transactions but important for monetary analysis.

questionBank.q: Nigeria's VAT rate was increased from 7.5% to a higher rate. The MOST appropriate immediate monetary policy response to resulting inflationary pressure would be:
opts: Reducing the MPR to stimulate growth and offset consumer spending reduction
Cutting the CRR to increase banks' lending capacity
Monitoring price movements and potentially raising the MPR if inflation rises materially
Buying government bonds to inject liquidity into the banking system
questionBank.exp: A VAT increase typically raises prices (one‑time inflationary effect). The CBN should monitor the impact and consider raising rates if it leads to sustained inflationary pressure.

questionBank.q: A banker needs to explain to an SME customer why their loan repayment instalments have increased, even though no contract change occurred. The MOST likely explanation is:
opts: The bank changed its pricing model arbitrarily
The customer is on a variable rate loan, and the CBN's MPR increase has flowed through to their lending rate
The CBN directly sets Access Bank's lending rates for individual customers
Inflation has automatically increased the nominal value of the loan
questionBank.exp: Variable rate loans are linked to the MPR. When CBN raises the MPR, commercial banks pass on the increase — variable rate borrowers pay more.

questionBank.q: The CBN raises the MPR from 26% to 27%. The expected sequence of effects through the economy is:
opts: MPR rises → exchange rate appreciates → exports increase → GDP grows
MPR rises → bank lending rates rise → borrowing costs increase → investment falls → inflation moderates
MPR rises → government taxes rise → fiscal deficit falls → money supply increases
MPR rises → bank profits fall → dividends decrease → stock market rises
questionBank.exp: The monetary transmission mechanism: MPR rise → higher lending rates → expensive borrowing → less investment/consumption → reduced demand → lower inflation.

questionBank.q: Which circumstance would be MOST appropriate for a government to run a deliberate budget surplus?
opts: During a severe recession with rising unemployment
When inflation is rising rapidly and the economy is overheating
When GDP growth is negative for two consecutive quarters
When public infrastructure is critically underfunded
questionBank.exp: A surplus budget withdraws money from the economy (contractionary fiscal policy) — appropriate when the economy is overheating and inflation is rising.

questionBank.q: The tools of fiscal policy are:
opts: MPR, CRR, open market operations, and liquidity ratio
Taxes and government expenditure
Money supply targets and interest rate ceilings
Exchange rate management and foreign reserve deployment
questionBank.exp: Fiscal policy tools are taxes (revenue side) and government expenditure (spending side). Monetary policy tools include MPR, CRR, OMO, and liquidity ratio.

questionBank.q: The tools of monetary policy include all of the following EXCEPT:
opts: Open Market Operations
Cash Reserve Ratio
Government expenditure on infrastructure
Monetary Policy Rate
questionBank.exp: Government expenditure is a FISCAL policy tool. MPR, CRR, OMO, and liquidity ratio are all monetary policy tools controlled by the CBN.

questionBank.q: An increase in government borrowing to finance a large deficit can create a 'crowding out' effect. This occurs when:
opts: Government spending creates so many jobs that there is a labour shortage
Government borrowing raises interest rates, making it more expensive for private businesses to borrow and invest
Banks lend too much to the government, causing foreign exchange shortages
The CBN must print money to fund the deficit, creating hyperinflation
questionBank.exp: Crowding out occurs when heavy government borrowing pushes up interest rates, raising the cost of private sector borrowing and reducing private investment.

questionBank.q: High and rising inflation in Nigeria since COVID can be addressed through which COMBINATION of policies?
opts: Lowering the MPR and increasing government spending
Raising the MPR (monetary) and reducing government spending (fiscal) to withdraw money from the economy
Printing more money and devaluing the naira
Reducing the CRR while raising taxes
questionBank.exp: Fighting inflation requires tightening — raising the MPR (monetary) to make borrowing expensive, and cutting spending (fiscal) to reduce aggregate demand.

questionBank.q: Nigeria's inflation is at 30%, the MPR at 27%, and 91‑day T‑Bill yield at 22%. A treasury analyst should note that:
opts: Real returns on T‑Bills are positive at 22%, making them excellent investments
Real returns on T‑Bills are negative (-8%), meaning the bank is losing purchasing power
T‑Bill yields above the MPR indicate the market expects rate cuts
The 22% T‑Bill yield is irrelevant because the MPR sets all rates
questionBank.exp: Real return = T‑Bill yield (22%) - Inflation (30%) = -8%. Despite the positive nominal yield, the bank's real purchasing power is declining.

questionBank.q: In the context of fiscal policy, 'automatic stabilisers' refer to:
opts: The CBN's automatic adjustment of the MPR based on inflation data
Government spending programs (like unemployment benefits) and tax systems that automatically expand during recessions and contract during booms without legislative action
The automatic balancing of the government budget at the end of each fiscal year
Market mechanisms that automatically correct supply and demand imbalances
questionBank.exp: Automatic stabilisers are built‑in fiscal mechanisms — welfare payments increase and tax revenues fall automatically during recessions, providing counter‑cyclical stimulus.

questionBank.q: The phrase 'too much money chasing too few goods' describes inflation. The MOST DIRECT way to address this using monetary policy tools is:
opts: Increasing government spending to produce more goods
Raising the MPR, increasing the CRR, and conducting open market operations to sell securities — all withdrawing money from circulation
Reducing the liquidity ratio so banks have more funds to lend
Devaluing the naira to reduce import costs
questionBank.exp: To address 'too much money,' the CBN uses contractionary monetary tools: raising MPR (reduces borrowing), increasing CRR (locks reserves), and selling securities (removes naira from banks).

questionBank.q: A government already running a large deficit decides to fund new infrastructure by borrowing abroad in dollars. The macroeconomic risk for Nigerian banks is:
opts: The infrastructure will compete with bank products
Increased external debt raises debt‑servicing obligations in dollars, straining forex reserves and potentially causing naira depreciation that weakens bank customers
Foreign lenders will take over Nigerian banks
The CBN will automatically raise the MPR in response
questionBank.exp: Dollar‑denominated external debt increases forex demand for debt service. This depletes reserves, pressures the naira, and creates macroeconomic instability — affecting bank customers' ability to repay.

questionBank.q: A 'balanced budget multiplier' concept suggests that increasing both spending and taxes by the same amount still stimulates the economy because:
opts: Higher taxes always stimulate consumer spending
Government spending has a larger multiplier effect than taxation — a N1 increase in spending generates more GDP than a N1 increase in taxes reduces GDP
Balanced budgets automatically eliminate inflation
Equal spending and tax increases have no net effect
questionBank.exp: The balanced budget multiplier is positive because government spending (multiplier > 1) stimulates more than the equal tax increase depresses.

questionBank.q: The CBN is concerned about overheating (growth at 7%, inflation at 18%). The appropriate monetary policy action is:
opts: Lower the MPR to support growth
Raise the MPR to tighten conditions, reducing demand and controlling inflation
Reduce the CRR to inject liquidity
Buy government bonds to inject money
questionBank.exp: Overheating requires contractionary policy — raising the MPR to make borrowing more expensive and reduce demand.

questionBank.q: When the CBN reduces the MPR, banks are expected to reduce lending rates. This action is intended to:
opts: Increase government tax revenue
Stimulate economic activity by making borrowing cheaper, encouraging investment and consumption
Reduce inflation by making money more expensive
Appreciate the naira
questionBank.exp: Lowering the MPR stimulates the economy by reducing borrowing costs. This encourages investment and consumption, increasing aggregate demand.

questionBank.q: A government that wants to reduce its budget deficit without raising taxes could:
opts: Increase spending
Reduce spending on non‑essential programs
Borrow more
Print money
questionBank.exp: To reduce the deficit with unchanged tax rates, the government must reduce spending. This is contractionary fiscal policy.

questionBank.q: When the CBN sells Treasury Bills through open market operations, the effect on Access Bank's balance sheet is:
opts: The bank's reserves increase, increasing its lending capacity
The bank's reserves decrease, reducing its lending capacity, as cash is transferred to the CBN for the T-Bills purchased
The bank's loans automatically increase
No effect because T-Bills are separate from bank balance sheets
questionBank.exp: When the bank buys T-Bills from the CBN, it pays cash (reducing reserves). The bank now holds T-Bills (earning asset) instead of cash. Lending capacity is reduced.

questionBank.q: Access Bank is analyzing the impact of a 2% increase in the MPR on its variable-rate loan portfolio. If 50% of the bank's ₦200 billion loan book is variable-rate, the annual interest income increase (assuming full passthrough) is:
opts: ₦2 billion (2% × ₦100 billion variable portfolio)
₦4 billion (2% × ₦200 billion)
₦1 billion
No impact because banks absorb MPR changes
questionBank.exp: Variable-rate portfolio = 50% × ₦200 billion = ₦100 billion. Interest increase = 2% × ₦100 billion = ₦2 billion.

questionBank.q: The central bank's decision to raise the CRR from 45% to 48% would MOST directly affect Access Bank's:
opts: Profitability — less funds available for lending, reducing potential interest income
Number of branches
Staffing levels
Marketing budget
questionBank.exp: Higher CRR means more funds are locked as reserves, reducing the amount available for interest-earning loans. This can reduce net interest income and profitability.

questionBank.q: The CBN's 45% Cash Reserve Ratio and 30% Liquidity Ratio together mean that:
opts: Banks can only lend 25% of deposits (100% - 45% - 30% = 25%)
Banks must hold 45% at CBN and 30% in liquid assets, leaving a maximum of 25% for lending and other assets
Banks can lend 75% of deposits
Banks cannot lend because all deposits are held
questionBank.exp: CRR (45% at CBN) + Liquidity Ratio (30% in liquid instruments) = 75% of deposits held in these forms. This leaves up to 25% for lending and other earning assets.

questionBank.q: A key driver of Nigeria's high inflation in the post-COVID period has been money supply growth. If the CBN wants to reduce inflation, the MOST effective monetary policy action is:
opts: Increasing the MPR and conducting contractionary open market operations to reduce money supply
Printing more money to meet demand
Reducing the CRR to increase money supply
Reducing the Liquidity Ratio
questionBank.exp: If money supply growth is driving inflation, contractionary policy (raising MPR, selling securities) reduces money supply, addressing the root cause.

questionBank.q: The central bank's decision to RAISE the Monetary Policy Rate (MPR) is MOST LIKELY driven by:
opts: The desire to stimulate economic growth by making borrowing cheaper
Concerns about rising inflation and the need to tighten monetary conditions
The desire to increase government revenue
Pressure from commercial banks to lower their funding costs
questionBank.exp: Raising the MPR is the central bank's primary tool for combating inflation by making borrowing more expensive.

questionBank.q: The CBN's open market operation of selling government securities has the effect of:
opts: Injecting money into the banking system
Withdrawing money from the banking system
Having no effect on money supply
Increasing the CRR
questionBank.exp: Selling securities: banks pay cash (reserves) for securities. Cash leaves the banking system, reducing money supply and tightening liquidity.

questionBank.q: The central bank's decision to lower the CRR would MOST likely be intended to:
opts: Reduce the amount of money in circulation
Stimulate the economy by increasing the funds available for banks to lend
Increase the cost of borrowing
Restrict credit growth
questionBank.exp: Lowering the CRR releases reserves, increasing the amount banks can lend, stimulating economic activity.

questionBank.q: The CBN can increase the money supply through open market operations by:
opts: Selling government bonds to commercial banks
Buying government bonds from commercial banks, injecting cash into the banking system
Increasing the CRR
Raising the MPR
questionBank.exp: When CBN buys securities, it pays cash to banks. Cash is injected into the banking system, increasing money supply.

questionBank.q: The CBN's CRR and Liquidity Ratio are BOTH used to:
opts: Increase bank profitability
Control money supply and ensure financial stability
Reduce government borrowing
Increase bank lending
questionBank.exp: Both ratios are prudential tools: CRR restricts lending capacity (controlling money supply), Liquidity Ratio ensures banks can meet short-term obligations (stability).

questionBank.q: The CBN's Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) is currently 45% for commercial banks. A bank has N100 billion in deposits. What is the MAXIMUM amount available for lending, and what happens if the CBN raises CRR to 50%?
opts: N55 billion available; raising to 50% reduces lendable funds to N50 billion, tightening credit
N100 billion available; CRR does not reduce lendable funds
N45 billion available; raising CRR expands lending capacity
N55 billion available; raising CRR to 50% is expansionary monetary policy
questionBank.exp: CRR of 45% means 45% must be held in reserve: N100B × 45% = N45B reserved, leaving N55B lendable. Raising CRR to 50% means N50B reserved, leaving only N50B lendable — less credit in the economy. This is RESTRICTIVE monetary policy.

questionBank.q: The CBN's MPR is currently 27%. A commercial bank borrows from the CBN at this rate. The bank must earn a spread to be profitable. If the bank's operational costs add 3% and it targets a 2% net margin, what is the MINIMUM lending rate it can offer clients?
opts: 27% — the MPR directly sets the lending rate
32% — MPR + cost spread + margin
22% — below MPR is possible for large clients
30% — MPR plus standard 3% spread only
questionBank.exp: Banks borrow from CBN at MPR (27%), must cover their own operational costs (3%) and earn a margin (2%): 27 + 3 + 2 = 32% minimum. The MPR is the FLOOR cost of funds for banks — their lending rates must exceed it by enough to remain profitable.

questionBank.q: Access Bank's economist notes that NPLs historically correlate with inflation changes with an 18‑month lag. The actionable insight is:
opts: The bank should ignore current inflation
Current inflation trends will affect NPLs in ~18 months — the bank can proactively adjust lending standards and provisions now
The correlation is irrelevant because each cycle is unique
The bank should stop lending until inflation is controlled
questionBank.exp: If the bank knows NPLs follow inflation with a lag, it can take proactive action before the impact arrives — tightening standards or increasing provisions.

questionBank.q: The balance of payments is best defined as what kind of record?
opts: A systematic record of a country's tax collections by state
A systematic record of a country's transactions with the world
A systematic record of a company's annual production output
A systematic record of a bank's individual customer transactions
questionBank.exp: The BoP is a systematic record of all economic transactions between the residents of one country and the rest of the world over a given period.

questionBank.q: In the balance of payments analogy of a country's single bank account, which transactions make up the 'in' side?
opts: Imports and outgoing foreign investment
Exports and incoming foreign investment
Domestic taxation and government borrowing
Domestic consumption and public spending
questionBank.exp: The 'in' side tracks money earned from exports and money coming in from foreign investment.

questionBank.q: In the balance of payments analogy, which transactions make up the 'out' side?
opts: Exports and money earned from foreigners
Imports and money spent abroad
Domestic taxation and government revenue
Domestic savings and bank deposits
questionBank.exp: The 'out' side tracks money spent on imports and money residents spend when travelling or buying abroad.

questionBank.q: If the 'in' side of a country's balance of payments exceeds the 'out' side, this is known as what?
opts: A deficit
A surplus
A recession
An inflation
questionBank.exp: When the 'in' side has more money than the 'out' side, this is called a surplus.

questionBank.q: If the 'out' side of a country's balance of payments exceeds the 'in' side, this is known as what?
opts: A surplus
A deficit
A recession
An inflation
questionBank.exp: When the 'out' side has more money than the 'in' side, this is called a deficit.

questionBank.q: Why is balancing the money coming in and going out important for a country's economy?
opts: It increases annual growth by a fixed percentage
It helps keep the economy healthy and avoids owing excessive amounts
It shortens the time needed to approve international loans
It raises the country's credit rating within a single fiscal quarter
questionBank.exp: Balancing money in and out helps keep the economy healthy; a large uncontrolled deficit can cause problems like owing large amounts.

questionBank.q: A country earns ₦40 trillion from exports and foreign investment inflows, while spending ₦55 trillion on imports and outbound payments in the same year. What does this represent?
opts: A balance of payments surplus
A balance of payments deficit
A perfectly balanced budget
An informal trade embargo
questionBank.exp: Spending (₦55tn) exceeding earnings (₦40tn) from other countries is, by definition, a balance of payments deficit.

questionBank.q: What is a potential consequence for a country that consistently runs a large balance of payments deficit?
opts: It can accumulate significant foreign reserves
It can accumulate significant external debt
It can accumulate a permanent trade surplus
It can accumulate a stronger domestic currency within weeks
questionBank.exp: A big deficit, spending more than is earned from other countries, can cause problems like owing lots of money.

questionBank.q: What is the general implication of a country consistently running a balance of payments surplus?
opts: It is similar to borrowing against the country's future
It is similar to saving for the country's future
It is similar to a company declaring bankruptcy
It is similar to a currency being devalued sharply overnight
questionBank.exp: A surplus is described as being like saving for the future, which is a positive position for a country.

questionBank.q: A Nigerian company pays a foreign supplier for imported machinery. Which side of the balance of payments does this transaction fall under?
opts: The 'in' side, since money is leaving the country
The 'out' side, since money is leaving the country
The 'out' side, since money is entering the country
The 'in' side, since money is entering the country
questionBank.exp: Paying a foreign supplier sends money out of the country — an import payment on the 'out' side.

questionBank.q: The current account of the balance of payments records which four categories of transactions?
opts: Portfolio investment, FDI, loans, and reserves
Goods trade, services trade, income, and transfers
Stocks, bonds, real estate, and fixed assets
Taxation, government spending, borrowing, and subsidies
questionBank.exp: The current account covers trade in goods, trade in services, income, and transfers between a country and the rest of the world.

questionBank.q: A current account surplus indicates what about a country's trade position?
opts: The country is importing more than it is exporting
The country is exporting more than it is importing
The country's currency is fixed against the US dollar
The country's central bank is raising interest rates
questionBank.exp: A current account surplus indicates a country is exporting more than it is importing, often seen as a positive economic sign.

questionBank.q: A current account deficit raises what kind of concern for a country?
opts: Concern about the country's ability to collect income tax
Concern about the country's ability to pay for its imports
Concern about the country's ability to regulate its banks
Concern about the country's ability to issue new currency
questionBank.exp: A current account deficit suggests a country is importing more than exporting, raising concerns about its ability to pay for these imports.

questionBank.q: A Nigerian worker abroad sends money home to family. Under which balance of payments component is this remittance recorded?
opts: The capital account, under fixed asset transfers
The current account, under transfers
The financial account, under portfolio investment
The financial account, under foreign direct investment
questionBank.exp: Transfers, such as remittances or foreign aid, are recorded under the current account.

questionBank.q: A foreign tourist pays for a hotel stay and guided tours while visiting Nigeria. Under which balance of payments component is this recorded?
opts: The capital account, under physical asset transfers
The current account, under trade in services
The financial account, under portfolio investment
The financial account, under foreign direct investment
questionBank.exp: Tourism spending is trade in services, such as tourism and consulting, recorded under the current account.

questionBank.q: A Nigerian company receives dividend income from shares it holds in a foreign company. Under which balance of payments component is this recorded?
opts: The capital account, under fixed asset transfers
The current account, under income
The financial account, under foreign direct investment
The financial account, under currency reserves
questionBank.exp: Income such as interest and dividends is recorded under the current account.

questionBank.q: Why does a persistent current account deficit worry policymakers even if a country's capital and financial accounts show strong inflows?
opts: It signals an oversupply of domestically manufactured goods
It signals reliance on imports that must eventually be paid for
It signals a permanent decline in the central bank's MPR
It signals an immediate collapse of the banking sector
questionBank.exp: A current account deficit reflects import dependence, raising concerns about the country's ongoing ability to pay for those imports.

questionBank.q: The capital account of the balance of payments primarily records what kind of transactions?
opts: Trade flows of goods and services between countries
International capital flows into financial and physical assets
Domestic government tax and spending transactions
Day-to-day retail transactions between local banks
questionBank.exp: The capital account accounts for international capital flows, including investments in financial assets like stocks and bonds, and physical assets like real estate.

questionBank.q: Which of the following would typically be recorded under the capital account?
opts: A payment for imported consumer electronics
A transfer of ownership of land
A tourist's spending on local restaurants
A dividend payment from a foreign subsidiary
questionBank.exp: The capital account includes transfers of ownership of fixed assets, such as land.

questionBank.q: A foreign investor purchases a commercial property in Lagos. Under which balance of payments component is this transaction most directly recorded?
opts: The current account, under trade in services
The capital account, under physical asset investment
The current account, under income
The financial account, under portfolio investment
questionBank.exp: Investment in physical assets like real estate is recorded under the capital account.

questionBank.q: Ownership of a factory building is formally transferred from a local firm to a foreign parent company. Which balance of payments component records this transfer of ownership?
opts: The current account
The capital account
The government's fiscal budget
The monetary policy statement
questionBank.exp: The capital account includes transfers of ownership of fixed assets, such as a factory building.

questionBank.q: How does the capital account differ conceptually from the current account?
opts: It tracks day-to-day trade and income, not capital flows and asset ownership
It tracks capital flows and asset ownership, not day-to-day trade and income
It tracks government tax revenue, not private-sector transactions
It tracks interest rate changes, not asset ownership
questionBank.exp: The capital account records international capital flows and asset ownership transfers, distinct from the current account's day-to-day trade and income focus.

questionBank.q: The financial account of the balance of payments primarily records changes in what?
opts: A country's ownership of domestic physical infrastructure
A country's foreign financial assets and liabilities
A country's annual government budget allocations
A country's population and demographic statistics
questionBank.exp: The financial account records changes in a country's ownership of foreign financial assets and liabilities.

questionBank.q: A foreign company builds a new factory in Nigeria to manufacture goods locally. This is an example of what, recorded under the financial account?
opts: Portfolio investment
Foreign direct investment
A current account transfer
A capital account grant
questionBank.exp: Building and operating a factory directly is foreign direct investment (FDI), a component of the financial account.

questionBank.q: A foreign investor buys shares of a Nigerian company listed on the stock exchange, without taking any management role. This is an example of what, recorded under the financial account?
opts: Foreign direct investment
Portfolio investment
A current account transfer
A capital account grant
questionBank.exp: Buying shares purely as an investment, without operational control, is portfolio investment, part of the financial account.

questionBank.q: A multinational bank opens and directly operates a new subsidiary branch network in Nigeria. Which financial account category best captures this investment?
opts: Portfolio investment
Foreign direct investment
Currency reserve accumulation
A loan repayment
questionBank.exp: Directly establishing and operating a business is foreign direct investment (FDI).

questionBank.q: An international pension fund purchases Nigerian government treasury bonds purely as a financial investment. Which financial account category best captures this transaction?
opts: Foreign direct investment
Portfolio investment
A current account transfer
A capital account grant
questionBank.exp: Purchases of stocks and bonds as pure financial investment are classified as portfolio investment.

questionBank.q: How does the financial account differ conceptually from the capital account?
opts: It tracks ownership changes in physical assets and fixed-asset transfers
It tracks ownership changes in stocks, bonds, and loans
It tracks government tax revenue and public spending changes
It tracks the current account's trade balance directly
questionBank.exp: The financial account covers FDI, portfolio investment, loans, and reserves, while the capital account focuses more on physical asset and fixed-asset ownership transfers.

questionBank.q: An exchange rate is best defined as what?
opts: The rate at which a government taxes imported goods
The rate at which one currency can be exchanged for another
The rate at which a central bank lends to commercial banks
The rate at which consumer prices rise over time
questionBank.exp: An exchange rate is the rate at which one currency can be exchanged for another.

questionBank.q: Why does the exchange rate play a critical role in international trade and finance?
opts: It represents the relative size of a country's population
It represents the relative value of one country's currency against another's
It represents the relative level of a country's literacy rate
It represents the relative height of a country's stock market index
questionBank.exp: The exchange rate represents the value of one country's currency relative to another's, playing a critical role in trade and finance.

questionBank.q: In a fixed, or pegged, exchange rate system, who sets the specific value of the currency?
opts: Market forces of supply and demand alone
The country's central bank or government
A private consortium of commercial banks
An international ratings agency
questionBank.exp: In a fixed exchange rate system, a country's central bank or government sets a specific value for its currency.

questionBank.q: How does a central bank typically maintain a fixed exchange rate?
opts: By raising or lowering domestic income tax rates as needed
By buying or selling its currency in the FX market
By adjusting the national minimum wage as needed
By changing bank branch operating hours as needed
questionBank.exp: The central bank maintains a fixed rate by intervening in the foreign exchange market, buying or selling its currency as needed.

questionBank.q: What is a recognized drawback of a fixed exchange rate system, despite the stability it provides?
opts: It tends to cause persistent double-digit inflation
It can be challenging to sustain over the long term
It tends to discourage most forms of international trade
It tends to double a country's foreign reserves within a year
questionBank.exp: A fixed exchange rate mechanism provides stability but can be challenging to sustain over the long term.

questionBank.q: In a floating exchange rate system, what primarily determines the currency's value?
opts: A fixed peg set by the central bank
Market forces of supply and demand
A rate negotiated annually with trading partners
A rate set by an international monetary body
questionBank.exp: In a floating exchange rate system, the currency's value is determined by market forces of supply and demand.

questionBank.q: In a floating exchange rate system, how actively do governments and central banks typically intervene to maintain a specific rate?
opts: They intervene daily to maintain a specific fixed rate
They do not actively intervene to maintain a specific rate
They intervene only during scheduled quarterly reviews
They delegate all intervention decisions to commercial banks
questionBank.exp: Under a floating system, governments and central banks do not actively intervene to maintain a specific exchange rate.

questionBank.q: Because a floating exchange rate responds to changing economic factors like interest rates and inflation, what characteristic does it typically display?
opts: Complete price stability over time
Frequent fluctuation in value
A single fixed value set annually
No relationship to inflation or interest rates
questionBank.exp: A floating exchange rate is a more flexible system, and rates can change frequently based on economic factors.

questionBank.q: A system in which the exchange rate mostly floats but the central bank occasionally intervenes to stabilize it is known as what?
opts: A fixed exchange rate mechanism
A dirty float mechanism
A pure floating mechanism
A currency board mechanism
questionBank.exp: A dirty float system involves occasional government or central bank intervention within an otherwise floating system.

questionBank.q: Under a dirty float system, why might a central bank occasionally intervene in the foreign exchange market?
opts: To lock the currency at a single value for a full decade
To stabilize the currency or prevent excessive fluctuations
To remove market forces from setting the rate each quarter
To transfer control of the currency to a foreign government
questionBank.exp: Under a dirty float, intervention can be used to stabilize the currency, prevent excessive fluctuations, or achieve specific economic goals.

questionBank.q: How does a dirty float mechanism differ from a pure floating exchange rate system?
opts: It involves constant government intervention, unlike a pure float
It involves occasional government intervention, unlike a pure float
It involves a rate fixed by treaty, unlike a pure float
It involves a rate fixed by law for one full year, unlike a pure float
questionBank.exp: A dirty float involves occasional intervention, distinguishing it from a pure float where the rate is left entirely to market forces.

questionBank.q: A bank's treasury team is planning its foreign exchange hedging strategy for the coming year. The central bank operates a dirty float and has a history of unpredictable interventions. What should this most directly encourage the treasury team to do?
opts: Assume the exchange rate will stay at today's level all year
Maintain flexible hedging positions to accommodate sudden central bank action
Ignore exchange rate movements since the currency floats freely
Rely on last year's average exchange rate without further review
questionBank.exp: Since a dirty float mixes market-driven movement with occasional unpredictable central bank intervention, treasury planning should stay flexible rather than assume either pure stability or pure market-driven predictability.

questionBank.q: Nigeria receives $20 billion in oil export revenues, $5 billion in diaspora remittances, and pays $12 billion for imported goods and $3 billion for services. Nigeria's current account balance is:
opts: Surplus of $10 billion
Deficit of $10 billion
Surplus of $5 billion
Deficit of $5 billion
questionBank.exp: Current account = Exports ($20B + $5B remittances) - Imports ($12B goods + $3B services) = $25B - $15B = $10B surplus.

questionBank.q: A Nigerian bank receives a $50 million investment from a German bank for an equity stake. This is recorded in Nigeria's Balance of Payments in the:
opts: Current account, as it represents income from abroad
Capital account, as it is a transfer of financial ownership
Financial account, as it represents foreign direct investment
Reserve account, as the CBN must hold the equivalent in reserves
questionBank.exp: Foreign Direct Investment (equity stakes) is recorded in the Financial Account.

questionBank.q: Nigeria consistently imports more than it exports in non‑oil trade, resulting in a persistent current account deficit. The MOST sustainable long‑term solution is:
opts: Devaluing the naira annually to reduce import volumes
Borrowing from the IMF to finance the deficit indefinitely
Building productive domestic capacity to reduce import dependence and grow non‑oil exports
Prohibiting all luxury imports through regulatory fiat
questionBank.exp: Persistent current account deficits are best resolved by structural improvements in domestic production and export capacity.

questionBank.q: Under a FIXED exchange rate system, if Nigeria's naira is pegged at N750/$ but market forces value it at N1,200/$, the CBN must:
opts: Allow the naira to depreciate freely to find equilibrium
Print more naira to meet excess demand for dollars
Sell dollars from reserves to support the naira at N750, depleting reserves over time
Raise interest rates so that equilibrium moves to N750
questionBank.exp: To maintain an overvalued fixed rate, the CBN must supply dollars from reserves to meet excess demand. This depletes reserves — a key sustainability challenge.

questionBank.q: Nigeria switched from a managed peg to a 'dirty float' exchange rate regime. The MOST ACCURATE description is:
opts: The naira floats freely with no government intervention
The naira is fixed to a basket with daily adjustments
The naira's value is primarily market‑determined but the CBN intervenes occasionally to smooth excessive volatility
The naira is pegged to the dollar but adjusted quarterly
questionBank.exp: A dirty float (managed float) means the rate is broadly market‑determined, but the central bank intervenes selectively to prevent disorderly movements.

questionBank.q: A Nigerian exporter (earning dollars) benefits from naira depreciation, while an importer (paying dollars) suffers. Sustained depreciation would be expected to:
opts: Worsen the current account by making all goods more expensive
Improve the current account over time by making exports cheaper and imports more expensive, encouraging trade rebalancing
Have no impact on the current account
Improve the capital account by attracting more FDI
questionBank.exp: Naira depreciation makes exports cheaper and imports more expensive — theoretically improving the current account through the price effect on trade.

questionBank.q: Which transaction would appear in Nigeria's CURRENT ACCOUNT?
opts: A Nigerian bank borrowing from a European bank for 5 years
A foreign company purchasing a 40% stake in a Nigerian oil company
The Nigerian government receiving a grant from the World Bank for a health project
Access Bank purchasing a property in London
questionBank.exp: Grants and transfers are current account items. Portfolio and direct investments are in the financial account. Bank borrowing is a financial liability. Property purchase is also financial account.

questionBank.q: Nigeria's foreign exchange reserves fell from $45 billion to $33 billion over 18 months while maintaining a fixed rate. A banker should interpret this as:
opts: A sign of economic growth — lower reserves mean more money in circulation
A warning sign — the CBN is depleting reserves to defend the fixed rate, which may not be sustainable
Normal fluctuation unrelated to exchange rate management
A positive sign — lower reserves mean less currency overvaluation
questionBank.exp: Falling reserves while defending a fixed rate is a classic warning sign of an unsustainable peg. Eventually reserves run out, forcing devaluation or regime change.

questionBank.q: Diaspora remittances ($20+ billion annually) are important to Nigeria's economy because:
opts: They are recorded in the financial account and increase government revenue
They contribute to the current account surplus and provide a relatively stable source of foreign exchange
They reduce Nigeria's need for any formal banking system
They are the primary driver of foreign direct investment
questionBank.exp: Remittances are recorded in the current account (as transfers). They represent a stable, countercyclical source of foreign exchange.

questionBank.q: A country has a current account deficit but a financial account surplus of equal magnitude. The overall Balance of Payments is:
opts: In deficit, because the current account is always more important
In surplus, because financial account inflows exceed current account outflows
In balance, because the financial account surplus finances the current account deficit
Indeterminate without knowing the exchange rate
questionBank.exp: The BoP must balance — a current account deficit must be financed by a financial account surplus (capital inflows). When equal, the overall BoP is in balance.

questionBank.q: A 'twin deficit' problem occurs when a country simultaneously has:
opts: A current account surplus and a budget surplus
A current account deficit and a government budget deficit
High inflation and high unemployment
A fiscal surplus and a financial account deficit
questionBank.exp: Twin deficits occur when a government budget deficit coincides with a current account deficit (imports > exports). Nigeria has historically experienced both.

questionBank.q: Nigeria's Balance of Payments Current Account shows exports of $45 billion and imports of $62 billion. The current account position is a:
opts: Surplus of $17 billion — Nigeria earns more from abroad than it spends
Deficit of $17 billion — Nigeria spends more abroad than it earns
Balanced position — the gap is covered by the financial account
Capital account deficit — investment outflows exceed inflows
questionBank.exp: Current account = exports - imports (simplified). $45B - $62B = -$17B, a DEFICIT. The course states a current account deficit means the country imports more than it exports, raising concerns about its ability to pay for those imports.

questionBank.q: Remittances sent by Nigerians in the diaspora to family members at home are recorded in which component of the Balance of Payments?
opts: Financial Account — because they involve cross-border money transfers
Capital Account — because they represent asset transfers between countries
Current Account — under transfers (remittances count as income transfers)
None — personal remittances are not captured in official BOP statistics
questionBank.exp: The course states the Current Account covers 'transfers (like foreign aid or remittances) between a country and the rest of the world.' Diaspora remittances are transfer payments — they flow into the Current Account, not the Financial or Capital Account.

questionBank.q: The CBN announces it will buy US dollars in the foreign exchange market to support the Naira's value. Under which exchange rate regime does this action constitute standard operating procedure?
opts: Floating exchange rate — governments never intervene in floating systems
Fixed/Pegged exchange rate — the central bank actively buys/sells currency to maintain the pegged value
Dirty float — the CBN occasionally intervenes to influence rates, consistent with a managed float
The CBN's action violates IMF rules under any exchange rate regime
questionBank.exp: In a Fixed/Pegged system, the central bank MUST buy or sell its currency to maintain the target rate — this is the defining mechanism. Dirty float intervention is occasional by definition, whereas this describes routine, systematic defence of a peg.

questionBank.q: A country records significant Foreign Direct Investment inflows (multinationals building factories). In which BOP account is this recorded, and does it represent a surplus or deficit in that account?
opts: Current Account surplus — FDI generates export revenue
Financial Account inflow — FDI increases a country's foreign financial liabilities (foreigners own domestic assets), contributing to a financial account surplus (positive)
Capital Account deficit — factories represent fixed asset transfer out of the country
Current Account deficit — FDI inflows must be balanced by importing capital equipment
questionBank.exp: The Financial Account captures changes in a country's ownership of foreign financial assets and liabilities, including FDI. When foreigners invest in domestic factories, it's an inflow (credit) in the Financial Account. The country's liabilities to foreigners increase, but this is a POSITIVE (surplus) entry as capital is entering.
